documents.text:
Let’s cut through one of the most common points of confusion for anyone moving to Spain. The DNI (Documento Nacional de Identidad) is the national ID for Spanish citizens. That's it.

If you’re a foreigner, your foundational document is the NIE (Número de Identidad de Extranjero). Think of it this way: your life in Spain begins with an NIE. If you eventually become a Spanish citizen, you’ll get a DNI.

Understanding the DNI Number Spain and Its Role

Need help with your case in Spain? Contact our team (https://legalfournier.com/en/contact/) for tailored guidance before you make a move.

In our experience, mixing up these two documents is the source of countless administrative headaches. They look similar and serve related functions, but they're for entirely different people. Getting this right from day one saves a massive amount of time.

The DNI is a mandatory ID card for every Spanish citizen over the age of 14. It's a physical, credit-card-sized document with a photo, a unique number, and a microchip. This single card is the key to almost every official transaction in Spain, from opening a bank account to voting.

DNI vs NIE: The Core Difference

The distinction is simple. The DNI is proof of citizenship. The NIE is an administrative number for foreigners. It’s a tool the Spanish government uses to track your financial and legal activities.

To make it clearer, here’s a quick comparison.

DNI vs NIE at a Glance

As you can see, your journey to a Spanish passport can take anywhere from one to ten years, depending on your circumstances. The DNI application is the very last piece of the puzzle after your citizenship is granted.

Gathering Your Documents

Once the appointment is secured, your next job is to assemble your documents. Showing up unprepared is the number one reason for a failed appointment. And a failed appointment means you're back to square one, hunting for another cita previa. In our experience, having every single document in perfect order is the only way to go.

Here's what you absolutely must bring:

Literal Birth Certificate for DNI: This is non-negotiable. It is not your original birth certificate from back home. It's a special document issued by the same Spanish Civil Registry where you took your oath. It must explicitly state it's for the purpose of getting a DNI (certificación literal de nacimiento expedida a los solos efectos de obtener el DNI).

Recent Photograph: One recent, color, passport-style photo (32×26 mm) against a plain white background. No glasses, no hats, unless a head covering is for religious reasons.

Certificado de Empadronamiento: Your town hall registration certificate, which proves your current address. Make sure it was issued within the last three months before your DNI appointment.

Proof of Fee Payment: There is a small official fee for the DNI appointment, and you should check the current amount when booking.

The practical point is to bring the specific birth certificate issued for DNI purposes after nationality has been granted, not just any older certificate already on file.

At the Police Station

On the day of your appointment, get there a bit early. Have all your documents ready. A police official will check your paperwork, take your fingerprints electronically, and process the application.

If all your documents are correct, they print your new Spanish DNI card and hand it to you right then and there. You will walk out of the police station with your official DNI in your wallet. The whole thing usually takes less than 30 minutes.

From this moment on, that card is your life. It contains your unique DNI number, which automatically becomes your new tax ID number (NIF). Your transition is finally complete.

Using Your DNI in Daily and Legal Life

Once you have your DNI, it becomes your master key for practically everything in Spain. This isn’t just another piece of plastic; it’s the document that shifts you from a resident to a full member of the civil and legal fabric of the country.

You'll use it to vote, sign a mortgage, and travel across the EU and Schengen Area, often without your passport. But here's where we see new citizens stumble: they are so relieved to finish the nationality process that they forget the final, important step.

Your old NIE number is now history for identification purposes. Your new DNI number has replaced it, and this number is also your new tax ID (NIF). You have to tell everyone. If you don't, you're setting yourself up for administrative and financial headaches.

Your Official DNI Update Checklist

Think of this as your post-citizenship homework. Skip it, and you risk problems with your tax returns, access to your bank account, and even getting your salary paid. We've put together a checklist of who you must notify as soon as that DNI number Spain is in your hands.

The Spanish Tax Agency (Agencia Tributaria): This is your number one priority. Your NIF has changed. You must formally report this change using Modelo 030 to update your official census data (censo de obligados tributarios). If you don't, your tax filings will be under the wrong ID, creating a mess that takes time to fix.

Social Security (Tesorería General de la Seguridad Social): All your contributions, access to public healthcare, and your future pension are tied to your identification number. Updating it ensures your work history and benefits are consolidated under your new citizen status.

Your Bank: Your bank accounts are still linked to your old NIE. Walk into your branch with your new DNI right away to prevent your account from being frozen over an ID mismatch.

Your Employer: Your company’s HR department needs your new DNI to process your salary (nómina) and pay your social security contributions correctly.

Utility Companies: Gas, electricity, water, internet, and your mobile phone provider all have your NIE on file. A quick update ensures your contracts and billing continue without issue.

We see this constantly. A client gets a letter from the tax office months after becoming a citizen, flagging an issue. The problem almost always traces back to one simple omission: they never filed the Modelo 030 to update their NIF with the Agencia Tributaria. It’s a five-minute task that prevents a five-month headache.

Practical Implications in Legal and Financial Life

Beyond the paperwork, your DNI fundamentally changes your standing. When you buy a property, the deed (escritura) will now be registered with your DNI. If you launch a business, your DNI identifies you as a founder or director.

Even simple day-to-day tasks are different. Picking up a certified letter from Correos or signing up for a gym now requires your DNI. It authenticates your identity with an authority your old TIE or EU green certificate never had. When you sign a document before a notary, they verify your identity against your DNI, confirming you as a Spanish citizen with full legal standing.

Taking care of these updates isn't optional; it's a non-negotiable part of the transition. It solidifies your new status and makes sure every part of the Spanish system, from tax to healthcare, sees you correctly. Our administrative team helps clients navigate this final step.

If you've recently become a citizen and want to make sure your transition is seamless, contact us for personalized advice.

Renewing or Replacing Your Spanish DNI

Your Spanish DNI has an expiry date. Just like a passport, it needs to be kept current. The process is usually simple, but knowing the rules—especially around renewal timelines and what to do if your card goes missing—is something every Spanish citizen needs to get right.

The validity period of your DNI is tied directly to your age. This is to make sure the photo on your card is a reasonably recent likeness.

Under 5: valid for 2 years; from 5 to 29: valid for 5 years.

From 30 to 69: your DNI is valid for 10 years.

From 70: valid for more than 10 years, with a stated expiry under RD 255/2025. Earlier cards retain their original validity, including previously permanent cards.

You can start the renewal process up to 180 days before the expiry date. Don't leave this to the last minute. We’ve seen clients get stuck when they discover that booking the required appointment (cita previa) can take several weeks, especially in busy cities.

How to Renew Your DNI

Renewing an expiring DNI is almost identical to getting your first one. You'll need to book an appointment at a National Police station (Comisaría de Policía) using the official Cita Previa website.

When you go to your appointment, you need to have these with you:

Your old DNI card: This is non-negotiable.

A recent photograph: One color, passport-sized photo (32×26 mm) on a plain white background.

Proof of payment: The fee is currently €12. You need the receipt.

If you've moved house since your last DNI was issued, you also need a recent certificado de empadronamiento. It must have been issued within the last three months to prove your new address. At the station, they’ll take your fingerprints, check your documents, and print your new DNI right there on the spot.

Replacing a Lost or Stolen DNI

Losing your DNI or having it stolen is more than an inconvenience; it's a security risk that requires immediate action to protect yourself from identity fraud.

Your first step is non-negotiable: go to the nearest police station and file a police report (denuncia). This creates an official record of the loss or theft, giving you a legal layer of protection. You will need a copy of this report to get a replacement.

We see this happen all the time, and our advice is always the same: report it immediately. In the wrong hands, a lost DNI can be used for all sorts of fraudulent activities. The police report is your proof that the card was out of your possession from that moment forward.

Once you have the report, book a cita previa to request a duplicate (duplicado). The appointment is the same as a renewal, but you'll present the denuncia instead of your old DNI. You'll still need the new photograph and to pay the fee.

The replacement card you receive will have the exact same expiry date as the card you lost. The only exception is if your lost card was set to expire within the next 90 days. In that case, you’ll be issued a new DNI with a full, fresh validity period.

Managing your dni number spain correctly is a basic administrative responsibility, whether it’s a simple renewal or dealing with the stress of a lost card.

If you’re facing any administrative hurdles in Spain, from residency paperwork to updating official records, contact us for a clear, practical solution.

Using Your Electronic DNI: Spain’s Digital Key

That little chip in your modern Spanish DNI isn’t just for show. It’s the core of the DNI electrónico (DNIe), a powerful tool that turns your physical ID into a secure digital key. With it, you can prove who you are and sign documents online with the same legal weight as a handwritten signature.

Frankly, most people we work with who learn to use their DNIe save themselves countless hours of administrative headaches. It’s your direct line to managing your official life in Spain without leaving your desk.

What Can You Actually Do with It?

Once your DNIe is activated, it lets you interact with almost any Spanish government portal. You'll need a basic USB card reader, but the time it saves makes the small investment worthwhile.

Here are a few practical things you can do:

File your taxes online. Access the Agencia Tributaria portal directly and securely without wrestling with complicated software logins.

Check government records. Log in to the Social Security (Seguridad Social) website to see your contribution history or check your driving record points with the DGT.

Sign official documents. Digitally sign employment contracts, rental agreements, or official forms with a legally binding signature.

The chip is activated at a machine in the National Police station when you collect your DNI card. You'll be prompted to set a secret PIN—don't lose it. This PIN is what you’ll use to authorize every digital action.

DNIe vs. Other Digital IDs

The DNIe is a solid option for online identity, but it’s not the only one. Many residents also use a software-based certificado digital (digital certificate) or the Cl@ve system.

A DNIe requires the physical card and a reader. A digital certificate is a file you install directly onto your computer or browser. Both get the job done, but the certificate avoids the need for extra hardware.

Spain’s population hit a record 49,442,844 as of 1 October 2025. With a foreign-born population of 9,825,266 (about 19.9% of the total), a huge number of long-term residents will eventually switch from an NIE to a DNI. These digital tools are essential.

Getting comfortable with these systems is key to navigating modern life in Spain. Our guide to the Cl@ve certificate and other digital tools (https://legalfournier.com/en/contact/clave-certificate/) is a good place to start.

If you need clear guidance on setting up your DNIe or other digital certificates for tax returns or official paperwork, we can help.

Common Questions About the DNI Number in Spain

Once you get your Spanish citizenship, the questions don't stop. They just change. Navigating the final step—the transition from a foreign resident with an NIE to a full citizen with a DNI—can be confusing.

Here are practical answers to the questions we hear most often from new Spanish citizens.

Does My NIE Number Become My DNI Number?

No, they are two completely separate identifiers. When you are granted Spanish nationality, the government formally deactivates your NIE. You are then assigned a brand new, unique DNI number.

This new DNI also becomes your new tax identification number (NIF). It's up to you to update this number everywhere it matters—from the Spanish Tax Agency (Agencia Tributaria) to your bank and utility providers.

Can I Keep My Original Passport and Have a DNI?

It depends on where you're from. Spain holds dual nationality agreements with most Ibero-American countries, plus Andorra, the Philippines, Equatorial Guinea, and Portugal. If your country of origin is on that list, you can hold both passports.

If your country isn't on the list, the standard procedure requires you to formally renounce your original nationality to get your Spanish one. This is a critical point, and getting clear advice before you start the citizenship process is vital.

For example, a citizen from the United States or the United Kingdom would typically be required to renounce their original citizenship. A citizen from Argentina or Mexico, however, would not.

How Long Is the DNI Valid For?

The validity period is tied to your age when the card is issued. The logic is simple: to make sure the photograph remains a reasonably current likeness of you.

Under 5: valid for 2 years; from 5 to 29: valid for 5 years.

From 30 to 69: valid for 10 years.

From 70: more than 10 years, with a stated expiry under RD 255/2025. Earlier cards retain their original validity, including previously permanent cards.

What Happens if I Lose My DNI Abroad?

Losing your DNI while traveling outside of Spain is a hassle, but there's a clear process. Your first move is to report the loss immediately to the local police in the country you're in. Get a copy of the police report.

With that report, head to the nearest Spanish embassy or consulate. They can't issue a replacement DNI card—that can only be done in Spain. What they can do is issue you a temporary travel document that allows you to fly back to Spain. Once home, you can apply for a replacement DNI at any National Police station.

Navigating the final steps of your citizenship journey, from handling dual nationality questions to updating all your official records, requires careful attention to detail. For clear, expert guidance tailored to your specific situation, contact us for personalized advice.

Contact our team (https://legalfournier.com/en/contact/)

documents.description: For many day-to-day tasks in Spain, a local bank account quickly becomes one of the most useful tools to have. It often makes rent, utilities, payroll, and routine payments much easier to manage. The process itself isn’t difficult, but it trips people up. The key is knowing which account type you qualify for and having […]
documents.text:
For many day-to-day tasks in Spain, a local bank account quickly becomes one of the most useful tools to have. It often makes rent, utilities, payroll, and routine payments much easier to manage.

The process itself isn’t difficult, but it trips people up. The key is knowing which account type you qualify for and having all your documents in a row before you walk into the bank. In our experience, preparation is everything.

Why You Need a Spanish Bank Account and Where to Start

Need help with your case in Spain? Contact our team (https://legalfournier.com/en/consultation-options/) for tailored guidance before you make a move.

Whether you’re moving to Spain to work, retire, or launch a business, a Spanish bank account is your financial hub. We’ve seen countless new arrivals try to get by without one, and it just doesn’t work. Landlords want a Spanish account for rent. Utility companies require it for direct debits. Simple things become major headaches.

Your first move is figuring out what kind of account to open. This depends entirely on your residency status, and it’s where most of the confusion starts. Let’s clear that up now.

Resident vs. Non-Resident Accounts

You have two main paths: a non-resident account (cuenta de no residente) or a resident account (cuenta de residente).

A non-resident account is intended for a customer whom the bank records as non-resident. A passport, NIE or residency card does not decide that classification on its own. The institution will ask for evidence and apply its current documentation policy.

A resident account is for a customer whom the bank records as resident after checking the relevant evidence. Ask the bank which documents it accepts and whether its terms or fees change when it updates the classification.

Here’s a quick comparison to help you see the difference.

Resident vs Non-Resident Accounts at a Glance

This table breaks down the two main account types for foreigners in Spain, helping you pinpoint which one matches your current situation.

Before you even start comparing banks, it is worth focusing on the paperwork. In practice, most delays happen at the document stage, and walking into a branch with an incomplete file is the fastest way to lose time.

Spanish banks are strict, largely thanks to EU-wide anti-money laundering laws. They aren’t being difficult for the sake of it; they are legally required to verify who you are, where you live, and where your money comes from. Get this part right, and the rest is easy.

The Non-Negotiables

Think of these as your ticket to even have a conversation with the bank manager. Without them, you won't get past the front desk.

Valid Passport: This seems obvious, but make sure it’s not expiring anytime soon. The bank will take a copy.

NIE Number (Número de Identificación de Extranjero): This is your all-purpose identification and tax number in Spain. Many banks will ask for it from the start, and even where a passport-only opening is possible, they will usually ask you to provide the NIE shortly afterwards.

Getting your NIE is often the first major hurdle for new arrivals. We manage this process for clients across Spain every day, navigating the appointment system and ensuring everything is filed correctly. If you don't have yours yet, it needs to be your top priority. You can learn more about our service for obtaining your NIE number in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/nie-number/).

Proving Your Resident or Non-Resident Status

For a non-resident account, the Banco de España (https://clientebancario.bde.es/pcb/es/menu-horizontal/podemosayudarte/criterios/Depositos_banca_405f8a0415fe661.html) says the bank must record the holder’s non-resident status and ask for proof within 15 days of opening. For a foreign individual, that proof is a negative residence certificate issued by the Ministry of the Interior no more than two months earlier. The bank must request fresh proof every two years and may block the account, after warning the holder, if the documentation is not supplied.

Opening is not automatic (https://clientebancario.bde.es/pcb/es/blog/solicitud-de-apertura-de-cuentas-de-pago.html): each institution applies its acceptance and anti-money-laundering checks. A bank may request evidence of the source of funds when the account is opened or later, and it may restrict access (https://clientebancario.bde.es/pcb/es/blog/cuales-son-los-tramites-para-abrir-una-cuenta-.html) if the origin of the money is not justified. Ask the bank what it requires for your circumstances and update the file when your status changes.

Proving Where You Live

Banks usually want a verifiable Spanish address. A temporary address on its own is often not enough.

Your two best options are:

Empadronamiento Certificate: Your official address registration from the local town hall (ayuntamiento). This is the gold standard.

Rental Contract: A signed lease agreement, usually for six months or longer, is also widely accepted.

Banks usually want recent proof of address, so it is sensible to request an updated certificate shortly before the appointment rather than relying on older paperwork.

Proving Your Financial Standing

Here's where many people get stuck. The bank needs to see proof of your economic activity. What you need depends entirely on your situation.

For employees:

A recent payslip (nómina).

Your Spanish employment contract (contrato de trabajo).

For self-employed (autónomos):

Proof of registration with the tax office (Modelo 036).

Recent social security payment receipts.

For students:

A letter of enrolment from your school or university in Spain.

Proof of a scholarship or other evidence that you have enough funds to support yourself during your studies.

For retirees or those not working:

Official pension documents showing your income.

Your last year's tax return from your home country often works well here.

The bank may require a sworn Spanish translation for documents issued in another language. Confirm the format with the institution before paying for a translation.

Choosing a bank for the transaction you actually need

Traditional and online banks use different onboarding and support models, but no provider is automatically best for every foreign customer. The practical questions are whether the bank accepts the person’s residence status, can review the source of funds and supports the property, company or immigration transaction for which the account is needed.

Ordinary fee and product comparisons are better handled through current consumer information. Legal Fournier’s review covers banking where it forms part of a wider Spanish property, company, immigration or source-of-funds matter.

When onboarding becomes a legal coordination issue

Banks may ask for identity, address, residence status, tax information and evidence explaining the origin and purpose of funds. The exact request depends on the institution and risk profile.

Legal coordination can help where a property completion or company funding date is approaching, a power of attorney is involved, immigration evidence is being used for onboarding, or the bank has blocked a material transaction. It does not guarantee that a bank will open or maintain an account.

Account status, tax reporting and blocked transactions

Customers should keep their residence, address and tax information current with the bank. Holding an account does not by itself determine tax residence, and reporting obligations depend on the person’s wider facts and assets.

For routine account use, consult the bank’s current terms and support. A paid legal consultation (https://legalfournier.com/en/consultation-options/) covers onboarding or a blocked transaction that affects a property purchase, company, immigration file or documented source-of-funds issue.

Frequently Asked Questions About Spanish Bank Accounts

Can I Open an Account Before I Get My NIE?

This is the classic chicken-and-egg problem for new arrivals. The short answer is sometimes, but it’s not ideal.

Some banks may allow a passport-based application, but document policies vary. The institution may request an NIE or other evidence during onboarding or later, so confirm the requirements before relying on the account.

Is It Possible to Open an Account Completely Online from Abroad?

Yes, absolutely. This is the standard model for online challenger banks like N26 (https://n26.com/en-es) and Revolut (https://www.revolut.com/es-ES/). Their entire process is built for remote, app-based applications. You can often get approved from your home country in minutes with just your passport and a smartphone.

Some traditional Spanish banks are starting to catch up, but their remote options often come with catches. The service might only be for citizens of certain countries, or it could be a special “online-only” account with different terms.

Getting a Spanish IBAN before you land is a huge advantage. It lets you handle rental deposits and other setup costs easily. The trade-off is a total lack of physical branches if you ever need face-to-face help.

What Happens to My Non-Resident Account When I Become a Resident?

Tell the bank when your residence, address or tax information changes and ask what evidence it needs to update your customer file. A TIE does not, by itself, determine every bank’s account classification.

The institution will confirm its process and whether the change affects the account’s terms or fees.

Do I Need a Spanish Phone Number?

Usually, yes. For everyday banking in Spain, a Spanish mobile number is often expected.

Banks use it for two-factor authentication every time you log in online or approve a payment. It’s a fundamental security measure, and they will not send verification codes to a foreign number.

We always tell clients: get a Spanish SIM card the day you arrive. You can buy a prepaid (prepago) SIM at the airport or any mobile phone shop. You’ll need it for your bank, government appointments, deliveries—pretty much everything.

Navigating Spanish banking on top of residency and tax rules can be a headache. The expert team at our firm offers personalised advice to make sure your financial setup in Spain is compliant and works for you from the very beginning.

Contact us (https://legalfournier.com/en/consultation-options/) and let us handle the details for you.

documents.title: Wills in Spain for Expats: 2026 Legal Guide
documents.description: For expats with property, bank accounts or other assets here, understanding wills in Spain is an important part of cross-border estate planning. A Spanish will is not mandatory merely because you own an asset in Spain, but a properly coordinated will can make the Spanish administration of the estate more efficient. The right structure depends […]
documents.text:
For expats with property, bank accounts or other assets here, understanding wills in Spain is an important part of cross-border estate planning. A Spanish will is not mandatory merely because you own an asset in Spain, but a properly coordinated will can make the Spanish administration of the estate more efficient.

The right structure depends on nationality, habitual residence, family circumstances, assets and any existing wills. The aim is to align the Spanish document with the wider estate plan—not to create a second will that conflicts with it.

When a Spanish Will Can Help With Assets in Spain

A foreign will may be valid in Spain, but using it can require probate evidence, an apostille or legalisation and a sworn translation. Whether a separate Spanish will is worthwhile depends on the estate. For some clients it simplifies the local process; for others, careful coordination of the existing will is the better answer.

The decision should follow a review of the documents and assets rather than a fixed rule that every foreign owner needs a Spanish will.

When considering how to manage your Spanish assets, the difference between using a local will and a foreign one is stark. Here’s a quick comparison to make the choice clear.

Spanish Will vs Foreign Will for Spanish Assets

| Feature
| Using a Spanish Will
| Relying on a Foreign Will

| Speed
| Fast. Probate often completed in weeks.
| Slow. Can take 12–18+ months depending on translations and the procedures required for the estate.

| Cost
| Lower. A one-time notary fee is the main cost.
| Variable. Translation, legalisation and other administration costs vary; court proceedings are not automatically required.

| Clarity
| Clear. Specifically addresses Spanish assets under Spanish format.
| Confusing. Spanish officials must interpret foreign legal concepts.

| Control
| Full control. You can elect your national law to avoid forced heirship.
| Risky. May unintentionally trigger Spanish forced heirship rules.

| Convenience for Heirs
| Simple. Heirs work with a local notary and lawyer.
| Burdensome. Heirs must navigate multiple legal systems while grieving.

Understanding Spanish Forced Heirship Rules

If you’re from the UK, the US, or another common law country, Spain’s forced heirship system will likely be your biggest surprise. We call it the legítima. It’s a default rule that can feel incredibly restrictive if you’re used to leaving your assets to whomever you wish.

Under the Spanish Civil Code, a large chunk of your estate is automatically reserved for specific relatives, known as “forced heirs” (herederos forzosos). You simply cannot give this portion to anyone else in your will. The system is meant to protect immediate family, but it often clashes directly with the intentions of expat clients — particularly those with blended families or a surviving spouse they want to protect.

Who Are the Forced Heirs?

The law sets out a very clear pecking order. It’s important to know who falls into this category, as it dictates how your estate gets split if Spanish law applies.

Children and descendants: Under the common Civil Code, they usually have the strongest reserved rights and come first in the order of succession.

Parents and ascendants: They can become relevant if there are no descendants.

Surviving spouse: The spouse often has usufruct rights rather than a simple outright share, but the exact outcome depends on the applicable law and family structure.

This creates situations our clients genuinely don’t see coming. We’ve worked with couples who assumed their Spanish apartment would pass smoothly to the surviving spouse — only to discover that, under default Spanish rules, adult children from a previous marriage were entitled to a forced share of that property. If you’re also planning to buy property in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/tax-finance/pitfalls-of-buying-property-in-spain/), understanding these rules before you purchase is far less costly than dealing with them afterwards.

The Three Thirds Rule Explained

Think of your estate as a cake sliced into three equal pieces. This is the core of Spanish inheritance and where it diverges completely from common law.

1. The Strict Legitime (Legítima Estricta): This first third is non-negotiable. It must be divided equally among your children. You have zero say in the matter.

2. The Improvement Third (Tercio de Mejora): This second third also has to go to your children or their descendants, but here you have some flexibility. You can “improve” one child’s inheritance by giving them the whole third, or split it unevenly.

3. The Free Disposal Third (Tercio de Libre Disposición): This is the only part you truly control. You can leave this final third to anyone — a friend, your spouse, a charity, or even give it as an extra portion to one of your children.

In practical terms, if Spanish law applies to your estate and you have children, two-thirds of everything you own in Spain is already spoken for by law. The exact result depends on the family structure and the law that ultimately applies to the succession — which is precisely why this needs to be assessed properly before anything is drafted.

How to Regain Control of Your Estate

Where the Regulation applies, nationality may provide a choice-of-law option. The EU Succession Regulation (No 650/2012) (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2012/650/oj/?locale=EN), also known as Brussels IV, is the key. It allows a person to choose the law of a state whose nationality they possess to govern their succession as a whole.

By adding a properly drafted “choice of law” clause to your Spanish will, you can ask for the law of your nationality to apply to your succession. That often avoids the default Spanish forced-heirship outcome — but the clause still needs to be coordinated with your wider estate and tax planning in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/tax-finance/taxes-for-expats-in-spain/). It is not a one-size-fits-all solution.

Without a valid election, the general rule is the law of habitual residence at death, subject to the Regulation’s exceptions and scope. If Spanish law applies, forced-heirship rules may affect the result. This is why the clause and the wider circumstances must be analysed together.

Choosing the Right Type of Spanish Will

When it comes to making a will in Spain, you have a few options. But for nearly every expat we work with, only one really makes sense: the Open Will. Its security, simplicity, and official registration make it the undisputed best choice. Other types of wills exist, but they often create more problems than they solve.

The Open Will (Testamento Abierto): Usually the Most Practical Option

The Open Will, or Testamento Abierto, is the most common and secure way to formalise your wishes in Spain. It’s the only type of will we prepare for our clients, and for good reason.

The will is signed before a public notary after being drafted by a legal expert. The notary verifies identity, capacity, and legal compliance. The original is held securely by the notary — and crucially, its existence is registered with Spain’s Central Registry of Last Wills (Registro de Actos de Última Voluntad). This means your will can never be lost, hidden, or overlooked. When the time comes, your heirs locate it with a single official search.

The Problematic Alternatives

While technically legal, the other types of Spanish wills are a minefield of risk, cost, and delay for the people you leave behind. We almost never recommend them.

The Closed Will (Testamento Cerrado): Submitted to a notary in a sealed envelope. What it says remains unknown until death — when the ordinary opening, verification and protocolisation procedure is handled by a notary; a dispute may require court proceedings.

The Holographic Will (Testamento Ológrafo): Written entirely by hand, with no notary. It must be presented to a notary within five years of death for verification and protocolisation; a dispute may require court proceedings. We’ve seen families spend more on the validation process than the testator saved by writing the will themselves.

An Open Will is often practical for Spanish assets, but the right instrument depends on the wider estate, family structure and any foreign will already in force.

How Spanish Inheritance Tax Works Across Regions

Spain’s inheritance tax, the Impuesto sobre Sucesiones y Donaciones, is not one single system. It’s a patchwork of rules set by the state and the 17 autonomous communities. The tax bill your heirs face depends entirely on where your assets are — and the difference between regions can be enormous.

State-level rates start at 7.65% and climb to 34%. But that’s just the baseline. The autonomous communities apply their own reliefs (bonificaciones) that can slash the final bill to almost nothing — or leave it largely intact. What this means in practice is that two families inheriting estates of identical value can face tax bills that differ by tens of thousands of euros, simply because of where the property sits. For a broader view of how Spain taxes residents and non-residents alike, see our guide to taxes for expats in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/tax-finance/taxes-for-expats-in-spain/).

The Impact of Regional Tax Differences

We see the consequences of this directly. Heirs in regions with generous reliefs can inherit large estates with minimal tax exposure. Heirs in regions without those reliefs can face five-figure tax bills on properties that were never intended to generate a tax burden. This is why we always review the regional tax position alongside the will itself — treating them as separate exercises routinely costs families money they didn’t have to spend.

Rules for Non-Resident Heirs

What happens if your heirs don’t live in Spain? For years, non-residents were forced to pay the higher state-level tax regardless of where the assets were. The European Court of Justice correctly ruled this was discriminatory.

A landmark decision now lets non-resident EU/EEA citizens use the more favourable tax laws of the autonomous community where the assets are located. This opens the door to significantly better outcomes for non-resident heirs — but the result still depends on the region, the family relationship, and how the estate is structured.

It’s not just about who gets what, but about how much they actually keep. If your heirs may eventually sell the inherited property, it’s also worth understanding capital gains tax in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/tax-finance/capital-gains-tax-in-spain-guide/) and how it interacts with your succession plan. To ensure your assets are positioned as effectively as possible, book a consultation with our team (https://legalfournier.com/en/consultation-options/).

What Working With Us Looks Like

Wills in Spain are not something you need to manage alone. The legal decisions involved — particularly around choice of law, family structure, and regional tax — require professional input. What we provide is a coordinated process that takes care of every element, so that nothing gets missed and nothing comes back to hurt your family later.

It starts with a conversation about your situation: what you own in Spain, who you want to benefit, and how that fits with any existing estate planning you have in your home country. From there, we handle the legal analysis, the drafting — including a bilingual version so you understand every clause — the coordination with a public notary, and the registration with Spain’s Central Registry of Last Wills. By the end of the process, your will is legally sound, properly registered, and impossible to overlook.

The clause that protects your freedom to distribute your estate as you choose, the language that prevents your Spanish will from inadvertently cancelling your home country will, the coordination with your regional inheritance tax position — these are the details that matter and the details we are paid to get right. To understand how our wills and inheritance service (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/wills-inheritance/) works in practice, get in touch.

When a Spanish will needs individual review

| Fact
| Question for review

| Existing foreign will
| Can both instruments operate without conflict?

| Assets in Spain
| Which assets and registrations will require Spanish administration?

| Residence and nationality
| Which succession rules and choice-of-law issues may apply?

| Family structure
| Do children, a spouse or a blended family create competing interests?

| Administration
| Will foreign records, powers or executors create delay in Spain?

The answers depend on the full estate and family position. Tax is a separate part of the analysis; see our guide to inheritance tax in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/tax-finance/inheritance-tax-in-spain/). Legal Fournier’s wills and inheritance service (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/wills-inheritance/) covers coordinated planning and administration.

Your Spanish Will Questions, Answered

Do I Really Need a Spanish Will for My Spanish Property?

Legally, no. Practically, the families who rely solely on a foreign will consistently face the most difficult and expensive probate processes we see. Sworn translations, apostilles, and notary procedures that drag on for months — sometimes well over a year — and cost thousands of euros in legal fees. A proper Spanish will makes the process far faster and far cheaper for the people you leave behind.

Can My Spouse and I Make a Joint Will?

No. Spanish law is very clear on this: wills are strictly individual. Each person must make their own separate will before a notary. Even if your wishes are identical, you will each sign your own Testamento Abierto. We can draft both wills together so they are fully coordinated and consistent with your shared estate plan.

What Happens If I Die in Spain With No Will at All?

If you die intestate in Spain, the law of your habitual residence determines how your estate is divided. If that’s Spain, rigid succession rules apply: children and their descendants come first, followed by parents or ascendants if there are no children. As for the surviving spouse — the position is more nuanced than most people expect. Under Spanish intestate law, the spouse does not inherit ownership rights alongside children or parents, but does retain usufruct rights over a portion of the estate: one-third when children survive, one-half when only parents survive. Full ownership only passes to the spouse when there are no living descendants or ascendants.

We’ve seen cases where a surviving spouse ends up with only a usufruct right while the deceased’s elderly parents — or adult children from a previous relationship — inherit the assets outright. On top of that, the heirs face a complex legal procedure called a declaración de herederos abintestato just to be formally recognised — adding more time and cost to an already difficult situation.

A coordinated will can record your wishes and reduce the risk of an unintended intestate outcome, subject to the law that ultimately governs the succession.

Planning your estate across borders raises questions that don’t have generic answers — they depend on your nationality, your family structure, your assets in Spain, and your wider succession plan. Our firm specialises in wills and inheritance services (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/wills-inheritance/) for expats across Spain. We work through these questions with you directly, so that nothing is left to chance.

documents.title: Your Guide to Pareja de Hecho in Spain for Expats
documents.description: For many international couples in Spain, the ‘pareja de hecho’ seems like the fastest route to residency for a non-EU partner. It’s a legal civil partnership that can appear much simpler than marriage, opening the door to the EU Family Member residency card. This is particularly relevant if you are an EU citizen planning to […]
documents.text:
For many international couples in Spain, the ‘pareja de hecho’ seems like the fastest route to residency for a non-EU partner. It’s a legal civil partnership that can appear much simpler than marriage, opening the door to the EU Family Member residency card.

This is particularly relevant if you are an EU citizen planning to relocate to Spain with a non-EU partner, or if you are already living in Spain and need to regularise your partner’s legal status.

But in our experience, this is not a simple ‘sign-and-go’ process. We see countless applications refused because of a single misunderstanding of the strict regional rules. A mistake here will waste months of your time, cost you thousands in lost opportunities, and put your legal status in Spain at immediate risk.

What Is a Pareja De Hecho and Is It Your Best Option?

This guide is written for EU and non-EU couples planning to live together in Spain, particularly where one partner needs to regularise their immigration status through the relationship.

Think of a pareja de hecho (also called a de facto partnership) as a formal, public registration of your stable relationship. It gives you and your partner certain legal rights and obligations, but it’s not the same as getting married. In our practice, this is often the most direct path for a non-EU citizen to gain residency through their EU partner.

The core benefit is clear: once your partnership is officially registered, the non-EU partner can apply for the Tarjeta de Familiar de Comunitario. This is a powerful 5-year residency and work permit.

Pareja De Hecho Vs Marriage: A Critical Comparison

It is essential to understand that a civil partnership is not just a “lighter” version of marriage. The legal implications are profoundly different, especially around inheritance, taxes, and how the partnership ends. For expats, getting this choice wrong can create serious financial and legal headaches down the road.

This table breaks down the main differences at a glance:

| Feature
| Pareja De Hecho (Civil Partnership)
| Marriage (Matrimonio)

| Residency Rights
| Grants the non-EU partner the right to apply for a 5-year EU family member residency card.
| Grants the non-EU partner the right to apply for a 5-year EU family member residency card.

| Tax Filing
| Partners cannot file joint tax returns (declaración conjunta). Each must file individually.
| Spouses can file joint tax returns, which can offer significant tax advantages.

| Inheritance Rights
| No automatic inheritance rights in most regions. A Spanish will is strongly recommended.*
| The surviving spouse has automatic inheritance rights (derechos legitimarios) by law.

| Pension Rights
| Entitlement depends on the applicable Social Security conditions; partners must also meet statutory formalisation and cohabitation requirements. There is no general financial-dependence requirement.
| The surviving spouse may qualify for a widow’s or widower’s pension if the applicable Social Security conditions are met.

| Dissolution
| Administratively simple. Can be dissolved by one partner registering the breakup. No court needed.
| Requires a formal, legal divorce process, which is more complex, costly, and time-consuming.

* In certain Autonomous Communities — including Catalonia, the Basque Country, Aragon, Navarre, Galicia, and the Balearic Islands — inheritance rights may be closer to those of marriage. The law governing the estate must be identified, especially in international cases.

While both provide a path to residency, the long-term financial and legal protections are not the same. Choosing the right one depends entirely on your specific situation and future plans in Spain.

Why The Details Matter

In our experience, clients who fail to grasp these distinctions face serious trouble later on. They secure residency but create future problems with tax authorities or family inheritance disputes. You can learn more by exploring our detailed guide on the differences between a civil partnership and marriage in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/diferencia-entre-pareja-de-hecho-y-matrimonio/).

In our firm, we repeatedly see clients who pursued a pareja de hecho for immigration benefits without considering the long-term tax and estate planning consequences. A successful strategy must address both from the very beginning.

Choosing between a civil partnership and marriage is a critical decision. The best option depends on your personal circumstances, your long-term goals in Spain, and, most importantly, the region where you plan to live. While a pareja de hecho can be an excellent tool, its power lies in correct execution. An error in judgment or procedure can turn this fast track into a dead end, leaving your partner with no legal status.

How Regional Differences Affect Your Pareja de Hecho Application

This is the exact point where most self-filed pareja de hecho applications fail. Many expats make the dangerous mistake of assuming Spain has a single, national law for civil partnerships.

It doesn’t. The reality is that each of Spain’s 17 autonomous communities sets its own rules. The requirements for registering a pareja de hecho in Barcelona are completely different from those in Madrid (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/pareja-de-hecho-madrid-requirements-residence/), Valencia, or Andalusia. This isn’t a minor detail—it’s the central reason applications are rejected.

The Regional Maze of Requirements

We see this mistake constantly. An American client living in Barcelona diligently follows a guide written for Madrid. The result is an immediate, costly, and entirely preventable refusal. You cannot afford this error when your residency is on the line.

Here are a few critical examples of how deep these regional divides run:

Madrid: The authorities here are strict. you must meet strict cohabitation requirements before you can even apply. Even a gap in your documentation may be sufficient grounds for refusal.

Catalonia (Barcelona): Catalonia offers specific pathways that can significantly accelerate the process — but their correct application depends entirely on your individual circumstances.

Valencia & Andalusia: These regions have their own specific demands. They often require a certain period of joint empadronamiento (address registration) or other specific proofs of a stable relationship that differ from both Madrid and Barcelona.

Failing to understand which set of rules applies to you is a critical failure that will halt your application. You could waste months gathering documents for a cohabitation rule that doesn’t exist in your region—or worse, file an application that is invalid from day one.

Securing Your EU Family Member Residency Card

Registering your pareja de hecho is not the final step. For most couples, it’s just the key that opens the door to the real goal: securing Spanish residency for the non-EU partner.

The prize is the Tarjeta de Identificación de Extranjero (TIE) as a family member of an EU citizen, also known as the Tarjeta de Familiar de Comunitario. This card is what makes the whole process worthwhile, turning a legal document into a life-changing reality. But once you have that pareja de hecho certificate, the clock starts ticking.

The Race Against the Clock

From the day your civil partnership is officially registered, you must move quickly — delays in filing the residency application can have serious consequences for your legal status. In our practice, this is where we see most self-managed applications fail.

A single mistake—a missing document, an expired certificate, or a poorly executed sworn translation—is enough for an outright refusal. This isn’t just a small delay. It means starting the entire process over, costing months of legal uncertainty. The non-EU partner can easily fall into an irregular immigration status, unable to work legally and living with the constant risk of removal.

In our experience handling hundreds of these cases, the transition from registering the partnership to filing the residency application is the most common failure point. Immigration officials are incredibly strict, and there is zero tolerance for incomplete or incorrect paperwork.

What the EU Family Member Card Gives You

The EU Family Member Card delivers full residency and work rights in Spain for five years — but it is the result of a process that must be executed without a single error. Successfully reaching this stage means your partner can live, work, and travel with full legal security. Getting there requires every step before it to be handled correctly.

This card is the end of immigration uncertainty. It’s the start of your life together in Spain on solid legal ground. To understand the specifics, our guide on the EU Family Member Card (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/eu-family-member-card/) breaks down the requirements in more detail.

Proving Financial Solvency Is Non-Negotiable

One of the most scrutinised requirements for the residency application is proof of financial means. The EU citizen must demonstrate they have sufficient funds to support the non-EU partner. This is not a suggestion; it is a mandatory condition for approval.

Ultimately, the pareja de hecho is a legal tool designed to secure the residency card. The process is a chain of connected steps, and if one link breaks, the entire chain fails—putting your future in Spain at risk.

Pareja de Hecho Spain: Key Legal Requirements

Registering a pareja de hecho is a legal procedure, not just filling out a form. In our experience, the single most common reason for refusal isn’t ineligibility—it’s a technical error with the paperwork.

Simply having a birth certificate isn’t enough. It has to be recent, correctly apostilled, and translated by a specific type of sworn translator officially recognised in Spain. One small mistake here can set you back months and force you to re-request and re-pay for documents from your home country.

Why Documentation Is More Complex Than It Appears

The process requires a complex set of legalised and translated documents that vary depending on your specific situation, nationality, and region of registration. There is no universal checklist that applies to every couple — and this is precisely where most self-filed applications collapse. A document that is valid in one region may be insufficient in another, and a single incorrect format can result in an outright refusal.

This infographic shows the simplified path from partnership registration to getting your residency card.

Don’t be fooled by its simplicity. Each of those three steps has its own strict rules and documentation requirements that can derail your application if not followed perfectly.

Choosing Your Path: Registry vs. Notary

Once your paperwork is perfect, you face a critical strategic decision: register at the regional public registry or before a public notary. This isn’t a choice of convenience. Choosing the wrong path can be a fatal flaw in your residency strategy.

This flexibility has come under fire. Following fraud investigations like Operación Carmín, authorities across Spain have been tightening the rules since early 2026. While certain regional pathways remain available, the requirements have tightened considerably and the correct approach depends entirely on your specific circumstances.

Getting this choice wrong means your application may lead to refusal. You’re forced to start over, having lost months of time, money, and effort. The stakes are simply too high to rely on guesswork or outdated forum advice. Your future in Spain depends on making the right strategic decision from day one.

Pareja de Hecho Residency Spain: Why So Many Applications Fail

It’s not usually a missing signature or a forgotten photocopy that gets a pareja de hecho application denied. The real problems are much deeper. What was once seen as a relatively simple path to residency has become a process full of traps for unprepared couples.

What makes this particularly difficult is the gap between what the law says and how officials apply it in practice. The regulations may state that a certain document is sufficient — but in our daily experience, we consistently see officials interpret requirements more strictly than the written rule suggests, or request additional evidence that no official guide mentions. That gap is invisible to anyone navigating this process alone, and it is exactly where applications fall apart.

In our practice, the most common failures aren’t about simple paperwork mistakes, but about failing to prove the one thing immigration officials now care about most: that your relationship is real.

The Authenticity Interview: A High-Stakes Test

After major crackdowns on fraudulent partnerships, like the infamous Operación Carmín, which led to a significant tightening of how applications are assessed across Spain, officials are on high alert. You can read more on how this has tightened the rules in these insights into Spain’s immigration trends (https://euroweeklynews.com/2025/05/07/spain-2025-from-residency-shortcut-to-bureaucratic-nightmare/).

This means you and your partner could be called in for separate, intensive interviews. They’ll ask detailed, personal questions about your life together, your history, and your plans. If your answers don’t match perfectly, your application won’t just be rejected. You risk getting flagged for fraud, which can poison every future immigration attempt you make in Spain.

This is where most people get into trouble. They have all the right documents, but they are not prepared for the interview. A small, innocent inconsistency is often read as deception, and the consequences for the non-EU partner can be devastating.

Fatal Errors We Help Our Clients Avoid

Beyond the interview, a few other critical mistakes sink applications all the time. Each one costs you time, money, and leaves a negative mark on your immigration record.

Here are the most common pitfalls we steer our clients clear of:

Not Enough Proof of a ‘Real Affective Link’: Signing the registration papers isn’t enough. Officials need to see substantive proof of an ongoing, genuine relationship — and what constitutes sufficient evidence is not always what couples expect. If you can’t build a convincing story of your life together, your application may lead to refusal.

Using the Wrong Address Registration Document: Your padrón is a critical legal document, not just proof of address. Using the wrong type of address registration document is one of the most common errors we see — and one that is entirely avoidable with proper guidance.

Trusting Unregulated Advisors (Gestors): It’s tempting to use a local gestor for help, assuming they’re a legal expert. Many are not qualified lawyers and simply do not have the immigration law knowledge for a complex case. We’ve cleaned up countless messes left by advisors who gave bad advice, filed the wrong papers, or missed crucial deadlines.

These aren’t small administrative issues; they are fundamental failures that can stop your life in Spain before it starts. It’s important to understand how these problems connect to the bigger picture of moving here. We cover this in more detail in our guide to the 7 biggest mistakes to avoid when moving to Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/7-biggest-mistakes-when-moving-to-spain/). Having an expert legal team means someone is watching out for every one of these potential disasters.

Secure Your Future in Spain With Confidence

The pareja de hecho process looks straightforward on paper. In practice, it’s a legal minefield where small mistakes have devastating consequences.

We see it all the time. A couple believes they have everything in order, but a single document is out of date or a regional requirement is missed. The application is refused. This isn’t just an administrative inconvenience. It means months of delays, the non-EU partner falling into an irregular status, and the loss of legal immigration status, the inability to work legally in Spain, and in some cases, the very real risk of forced separation.

This Is Not a DIY Project

A pareja de hecho application is not a checklist to be downloaded from a forum. It is a formal legal process with rules that are strict and unforgiving. Your right to build a life together in Spain is too important to risk on outdated information or a guess.

At Legal Fournier, our work is based on navigating this system every day for international clients like you. We remove the uncertainty.

At Legal Fournier, we navigate this system every day for international clients. Our work is based on getting the details right — because in this process, the details determine the outcome.

Don’t Let a Refusal Define Your Future

The most common mistake is waiting until something has already gone wrong. Every week spent trying to figure it out alone is another week your partner cannot work, travel freely, or feel secure. It’s time, money, and peace of mind you will never get back.

Don’t let a preventable bureaucratic error determine the future of your relationship. Your ability to build a life together in Spain is on the line. Stop guessing.

Talk to a Spanish lawyer (https://legalfournier.com/en/consultation-options/)

Frequently Asked Questions

The pareja de hecho process seems simple on the surface, but the details that separate a successful residency application from a refusal are often buried in regional laws and procedural nuances. Here are the questions we handle most often in our practice.

Do We Have to Live Together Before Registering a Pareja de Hecho?

This is one of the most critical questions, and the answer depends entirely on where in Spain you register. Requirements vary significantly by region and may depend on additional factors specific to your personal circumstances. What appears straightforward in one region may have important exceptions or alternative routes in another — and identifying which applies to your case requires professional assessment, not a general guide.

What Happens to My Residency if the Pareja de Hecho Ends?

Your residency status is immediately in jeopardy. When a pareja de hecho is dissolved, the EU Family Member Card tied to it can be revoked. You do not automatically keep your right to stay in Spain.

However, in certain circumstances it may be possible to maintain your residency. The specific grounds depend on factors such as the duration of the relationship and your personal situation. This requires swift and correct legal action — and it is an area where early professional guidance makes a significant difference.

Are Inheritance and Tax Rights the Same as in a Marriage?

No, they are not. This is a common and costly assumption. Treating a pareja de hecho like a marriage for financial purposes leads to serious, unexpected consequences.

A critical difference is that partners in a pareja de hecho cannot file a joint tax return (declaración conjunta). This frequently results in a significantly higher tax burden compared to married couples. Inheritance rights depend on the law governing the estate; qualifying surviving stable partners have statutory rights under Catalan law. Without a properly drafted Spanish will, your partner could be left with nothing.

This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Every case involves specific facts and circumstances that may affect the outcome. Legal Fournier recommends seeking professional legal guidance before taking any action based on the information contained in this article.

Don’t let a simple misunderstanding of the rules derail your future in Spain. The time to get expert legal guidance is now, before a mistake costs you months of delay and uncertainty. The team at Legal Fournier has the experience to guide you through every step, ensuring your application is not just correct, but strategic. Talk to a Spanish lawyer (https://legalfournier.com/en/consultation-options/) before you submit the file. Let us take the risk out of the process and build the clear, secure path for you and your partner to begin your life in Spain.

documents.title: ENISA España: Your Guide to Securing Startup Funding in Spain
documents.description: ENISA España does two jobs that are easy to confuse. It provides participative loans to startups and small businesses, and it certifies companies that qualify as an empresa emergente under Spain’s Startup Law. These are separate applications with different results. A loan is repayable financing. Certification is an administrative status that can give access to […]
documents.text:
ENISA España does two jobs that are easy to confuse. It provides participative loans to startups and small businesses, and it certifies companies that qualify as an empresa emergente under Spain’s Startup Law. These are separate applications with different results. A loan is repayable financing. Certification is an administrative status that can give access to statutory benefits.

The figures and conditions below come from ENISA’s financing and certification pages and article 7 of Ley 28/2022. ENISA reviews its financing amounts, so the official page should be checked again before an application is filed.

ENISA España financing: amounts and general conditions

ENISA currently offers participative loans from €25,000 to €1,500,000. It does not take a management role or an ownership stake through the loan. ENISA describes the product as being provided without guarantees, with the project and the management team’s solvency supporting its assessment.

The applicant must have its registered office and main activity in Spain. Its own funds must at least equal the amount requested. ENISA also requires a viable, innovative project with a competitive advantage. Meeting those baseline conditions makes an application possible; it does not promise approval.

The published opening fee is 0.5%, with quarterly payments. The general repayment term can run for up to seven years, including a principal grace period of up to two years. During that grace period the company pays interest but does not repay principal. The offer and signed agreement set the terms for the individual operation.

Interest on a participative loan

The interest has two components. ENISA describes the first as one-year Euribor plus a differential set for the operation. The second depends on the company’s financial performance. If the relevant profitability measure is negative, ENISA says that second component is zero for the period.

The company must provide the annual accounts needed for the calculation. A loan without conventional guarantees is still a loan, not a grant, and the borrower remains bound by the signed repayment and reporting terms.

The official ENISA financing page (https://www.enisa.es/servicios/financiacion/) contains the live conditions and application route.

ENISA startup certification

Certification is a free administrative process managed by ENISA. It is available to a company or cooperative, not to someone applying only as an individual self-employed worker.

The following is a non-exhaustive summary of ENISA’s headline requirements. Applicants should check the full official list before filing:

The company or cooperative must generally be no more than five years old, or seven years old in the sectors covered by the extended period.

It must have its registered office or a permanent establishment in Spain.

If it has employees, at least 60% of the workforce must have employment contracts in Spain.

The project must be innovative and scalable.

The company must not be listed on a regulated market.

It must not have distributed dividends.

Annual turnover must not exceed €10 million.

ENISA’s full requirements page (https://www.enisa.es/servicios/certificacion/requisitos/) includes other conditions concerning corporate restructurings, company groups, tax and Social Security compliance, disqualifications and significant environmental harm. ENISA may request more documents or information before issuing its resolution. The official certification page (https://www.enisa.es/servicios/certificacion/) provides the application route and the 2026 guidance.

The 15% tax rate is limited

Certification does not create a permanent 15% corporate income tax rate. Under article 7 of Ley 28/2022, the reduced rate applies in the first tax period in which the certified startup has a positive taxable base and in the next three tax periods. The company must retain its empresa emergente status throughout.

The company’s position still needs to be checked for each period. The rule appears in article 7 of Ley 28/2022 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2022-21739#a7).

Financing and certification are not interchangeable

| | ENISA financing | Startup certification

| Purpose | Participative loan funding | Recognition under the Startup Law

| Amount or limit | €25,000 to €1,500,000 | No loan amount; turnover must not exceed €10 million

| Spain connection | Registered office and main activity in Spain | Registered office or permanent establishment in Spain

| Financial test | Own funds at least equal to the amount requested | Certification criteria include turnover and dividend limits

| Outcome | A contractual loan, if approved | An administrative certification, if approved

A company may apply for both services, but a financing decision is not a certification decision, and certification is not a commitment to lend.

Preparing the right ENISA application

Start by deciding which service the company needs. A financing review should test the proposed amount against the live range, own funds and the company’s activity in Spain. A certification review should cover the incorporation date, legal form, Spanish establishment, workforce, dividends, turnover and the project’s innovative and scalable character.

Historical programme names, old amount caps and processing-time estimates are a poor basis for a filing. Use ENISA’s live pages and then read the actual resolution or contract issued for the company.

Common questions

Is ENISA financing a grant?

No. It is a participative loan, and the company remains responsible for the obligations in the signed agreement.

Does a loan automatically produce startup certification?

No. Financing and certification have different applications, criteria and outcomes.

Does certification guarantee a permanent 15% tax rate?

No. Article 7 limits the reduced rate to the first positive-taxable-base period and the following three periods, while the company retains startup status.

Legal Fournier recommends seeking professional legal guidance before taking any action based on the information contained in this article.
