documents.title: Spanish Immigration Lawyer: Visa & Tax Strategy for Expats
documents.description: You may be in that familiar position already. You have identified a visa category, downloaded a checklist, perhaps spoken to a gestor or relocation adviser, and concluded that what you need is a Spanish immigration lawyer to file the papers and move on. In practice, that assumption is where many applications start to lose ground. […]
documents.text:
You may be in that familiar position already. You have identified a visa category, downloaded a checklist, perhaps spoken to a gestor or relocation adviser, and concluded that what you need is a Spanish immigration lawyer to file the papers and move on.

In practice, that assumption is where many applications start to lose ground.

Spain’s regulated migration framework was reshaped by the Startup Law (Ley 28/2022, de 21 de diciembre (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2022-21739)), which created the Digital Nomad Visa and amended the special regime for inbound workers under article 93 of the Personal Income Tax Act. The substantive immigration framework was restructured again by the new Reglamento approved by Real Decreto 1155/2024 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2024-24099), in force since 20 May 2025, which replaced the previous Reglamento de Extranjería and reorganised several core authorisations.

In 2026 the system is more interconnected and more aggressively cross-checked between the Tax Agency, the Social Security Treasury and the Foreign Affairs Office than it was when most public guides were written. Demand has risen, but so has scrutiny: a poorly framed file is flagged faster than ever, and inconsistencies between the immigration story and the tax footprint can surface within weeks of submission.

A Spanish immigration lawyer should do far more than submit forms. The role involves structuring the case correctly, anticipating how officials will read it, and aligning immigration strategy with tax, timing and documentation from the start.

Table of contents

The true role of a Spanish immigration lawyer (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/spanish-immigration-lawyer/#the-true-role)

Why your visa strategy must include tax planning (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/spanish-immigration-lawyer/#visa-strategy-tax)

How to choose your legal partner in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/spanish-immigration-lawyer/#choose-legal-partner)

Common application pitfalls in practice (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/spanish-immigration-lawyer/#application-pitfalls)

Understanding legal scope and application timelines (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/spanish-immigration-lawyer/#legal-scope-timelines)

Frequently asked questions (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/spanish-immigration-lawyer/#faq)

Your next step (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/spanish-immigration-lawyer/#next-step)

The true role of a Spanish immigration lawyer

A professional accepts a role in Madrid, relocates with a spouse, and assumes the visa is the main decision. It rarely is.

The first strategic mistake usually happens earlier, when the applicant chooses an immigration route without checking how income, corporate structure, family dependency and future tax residence fit together under Spanish law.

Spain’s immigration system is legal, administrative and evidential at the same time. An applicant may satisfy the rule on paper and still file a weak case because the documents do not support the legal theory clearly enough, the wrong permit was chosen, or a tax fact was ignored that later creates inconsistencies the authority will read against the applicant.

A strong Spanish immigration lawyer does more than collect forms. Counsel tests whether the case fits the right route, identifies weaknesses before filing, and presents the application in a way that answers the authority’s likely objections before they are raised.

The strongest immigration file is usually the one that looks inevitable once an officer opens it.

Case design and authority-facing work

Applicants who could probably qualify often need the file rebuilt before submission. Income is shown in a format the authority does not find persuasive. Remote work evidence points in one direction while the chosen visa points in another.

Family applications often fail because dependency is assumed rather than evidenced under the criteria of the LO 4/2000 and the new Reglamento aprobado por RD 1155/2024.

Counsel also handles procedure with intent. Licensed lawyers in Spain can file digitally through professional channels, track developments more closely, and respond to administrative requests within their statutory deadlines with greater control. Speed and accuracy matter, but the real advantage is the lower risk of an avoidable refusal. Once a refusal has been issued, the path back is usually administrative appeal under Ley 39/2015, and the doctrine consolidated by the Sentencia del Tribunal Supremo 731/2023, de 5 de junio (Sala Tercera, recurso 1843/2022) is increasingly relevant: the Tribunal Supremo confirmed that limitations on the fundamental rights of foreign nationals require organic-law backing and cannot rest on mere regulatory or operational practice. The doctrine reinforces the substantive defensibility of cases where administrative scrutiny crosses into rights the regulation alone cannot lawfully restrict.

This matters more in cases that cross into tax.

An immigration file can look acceptable until someone asks where the applicant is paid, how services are invoiced, whether a foreign company is involved, or how many days the person expects to spend in Spain. Those facts shape permit choice, supporting evidence, and the advice that should be given before the application is ever submitted.

Clients considering remote work or relocation usually need immigration advice tied to tax planning for expats in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/tax-finance/taxes-for-expats-in-spain/), not a form-filling service with a narrow brief.

What experienced counsel changes

A document service checks whether papers exist. A lawyer focuses on whether those papers prove the necessary legal point.

That difference decides difficult cases. Foreign income, mixed employment arrangements, prior stays in Spain, dependent relatives, company ownership and cross-border tax exposure all require judgment calls.

At Legal Fournier, those files are treated as legal strategy matters, because a visa approved on the wrong assumptions can create larger problems after arrival — problems that often surface only when tax and Social Security data are reconciled the following fiscal year.

Why your visa strategy must include tax planning

A residence permit is only part of the move.

The day your immigration matter is approved, your tax issues do not begin later. In many cases, they have already begun.

For non-Spanish-speaking expats, this is the gap that causes the most expensive surprises. They secure the visa, relocate, and only then realise that the way they structured their work, invoicing, payroll or presence in Spain creates tax consequences their immigration adviser never addressed.

The Digital Nomad Visa is the obvious example

The Digital Nomad Visa, introduced by the Startup Law and currently regulated under articles 61 to 71 of Ley 14/2013 (as amended by Ley 28/2022), attracts remote workers for good reason.

It is also where fragmented advice causes the most confusion, because the visa may be viable while the tax position is not, or the reverse may be true.

The Beckham regime under article 93 LIRPF (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2006-20764) can be combined with a DNV in certain cases, but the eligibility analysis is more demanding than most applicants assume. The option must be exercised within a strict statutory window: under article 119 of the Reglamento del IRPF, the application has to be filed within six months from registration with Spanish Social Security or, where applicable, from the alta in the corresponding regime for the inbound activity.

Hybrid files are precisely where the analysis goes wrong: remote employment of a foreign company, partial self-employment in Spain, founder roles in non-Spanish entities. In all of those, the immigration route and the tax position need to be designed together rather than in sequence.

For a practical overview of the tax side, see our guidance on taxes for expats in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/tax-finance/taxes-for-expats-in-spain/).

Where applicants misjudge the risk

The recurrent problem is rarely that a client has done something obviously wrong.

More often, they have done something partially right in two separate silos. The visa application was prepared one way. Their payroll, invoicing or relocation timeline was planned another way.

Those two stories then collide once the authorities reconcile their information.

A workable immigration route can become a poor relocation decision if the tax treatment is ignored.

Typical pressure points include:

Remote work evidence: the immigration file may describe one working model, while the tax facts suggest another.

Timing of entry and filing: a few weeks can matter when residence, payroll and tax obligations need to align, particularly given the six-month window of article 119 RIRPF to opt for the special inbound regime.

Employer structure: employees, contractors, founders and shareholders do not present the same risk profile under either immigration or tax law.

Beckham Law assumptions: many applicants assume they qualify because they are moving for work. That assumption often does not survive a closer reading of article 93 LIRPF and its regulatory development.

This is why an integrated review matters before filing, not after approval. Once a residence permit has been granted on the wrong tax assumption, the structural error is rarely correctable without losing time, optionality, or the special regime altogether.

What a paid case review decides

The first review should decide whether the proposed immigration route fits the client’s actual life, work and family structure. Five questions usually control that decision:

What is the person’s current status in Spain or abroad?

What result do they need now, and what should remain possible later?

Is there a refusal, expiry date or other live deadline?

How do work, income and accompanying family members fit the route?

Will Spanish tax residence or the Beckham Law (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/beckham-law/) affect the move?

The consultation supplies the fact-specific answer. The article can only show why those questions need to be asked together.

Watch: Spanish Immigration Lawyer: When Do You Actually Need One? (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DGchnucg8eg) — Legal Fournier.

Where apparently simple applications become risky

Most avoidable problems come from route selection, inconsistent evidence, poor timing or a conflict between immigration and tax facts. Local filing practice can add another issue, especially when foreign records or a previous immigration history are involved.

Legal Fournier reviews these interactions across Digital Nomad Visa (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/digital-nomad-visa/), nationality (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/spanish-nationality-residence/), family reunification (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/family-reunification/) and appeals (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/appeals/) matters. A paid review is designed to identify which service, if any, matches the case before work begins.

Understanding legal scope and application timelines

Fees and timing are legitimate questions, but they are often asked too narrowly. The meaningful distinction between providers is scope, not price.

A salaried employee transferring within a multinational and a founder with mixed international income, dependents and prior stays in Spain are not buying the same legal service, even if both are filing under the same generic label.

What clients should evaluate

A useful way to assess any engagement letter is to ask what is included.

| Point to check
| Why it matters

| Scope of legal review
| Some providers price only submission, not strategy, document analysis or pre-filing diagnosis.

| Tax input
| Critical where the move changes residence under article 9 LIRPF or affects special regime eligibility.

| Follow-up work
| Clarifications and authority responses often determine the real workload.

| Coordination across disciplines
| Immigration, tax, Social Security and corporate questions rarely sit in separate files in practice.

On timing, no responsible lawyer should promise an exact approval date. What experienced counsel can do is reduce avoidable delay by filing a coherent application, anticipating queries and avoiding defects that trigger administrative returns or refusals.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a Spanish immigration lawyer or is a gestor sufficient?

A gestor can lodge documentation, but does not provide legal qualification of the case and is not the right interlocutor when the file involves cross-border tax exposure or atypical income. The practical answer depends on the overall consistency of the applicant’s position. As soon as there is a foreign company in the picture, dependents, prior stays in Spain or potential eligibility for a special regime, the file is no longer a documentation exercise and should not be treated as one.

How does the Beckham Law six-month deadline interact with my visa start date?

The option to apply for the special inbound regime under article 93 LIRPF must be exercised within six months from registration with Spanish Social Security, under article 119 of the Reglamento del IRPF. The window is rigid and runs from the formal alta date, not from arrival in Spain or from the visa stamp. For employees, the trigger is registration with the General Regime of Social Security. For self-employed inbound profiles, including many Digital Nomad Visa holders operating as autónomos, the regulatory trigger is typically the date of the residence authorisation or the alta censal with the Tax Agency, whichever applies first. In hybrid relocation scenarios, whether the option holds up under later review usually comes down to documentation choices made in the first weeks, not to remediation attempted afterwards.

Can I switch from a Digital Nomad Visa to another residence permit later?

Modifications and renewals are contemplated by the Ley 14/2013 framework and by the new Reglamento aprobado por RD 1155/2024, but the analysis is fact-specific. Whether a switch is viable depends on the underlying activity, on the time elapsed in the original status and on the consistency of the file with the new pathway. The defensibility of any modification depends on the documentary trail supporting the new legal theory rather than quietly contradicting the previous one, which almost always needs to be assessed before any change is filed.

What happens if my immigration file conflicts with my tax filing in Spain?

Inconsistencies between the immigration evidence and the tax position declared to AEAT are increasingly identified through automated reconciliation across administrations. Depending on the magnitude, the consequences range from informal information requests to formal regularisation procedures. The defensibility of the file under that kind of scrutiny depends on the overall consistency of the original strategy, which is again why the route choice and the tax position should sit on the same desk before filing rather than after.

Are foreign documents always valid for Spanish residence applications?

They are not automatically valid. Documents must comply with apostille or consular legalisation rules, must respect the validity periods Spanish authorities apply, and where required must be accompanied by a sworn translation. Errors at this stage are common and easy to underestimate. The country of origin, the document type and the specific procedure all change the analysis, and refusals on this basis are typically avoidable with proper preparation rather than recoverable once the file has been returned.

Does my Spanish residence permit automatically include public healthcare?

It does not. The residence authorisation governs immigration status. Access to the National Health System is determined separately, through registration with the Tesorería General de la Seguridad Social (TGSS) under the regime that fits the activity: Régimen General for employees, RETA for the self-employed, or convenio especial in some cases. Many newly arrived residents discover the gap when they first try to register with their local health centre. The defensibility of the position depends on the activity profile and on whether private healthcare coverage was used at the visa stage, since that carries its own continuity considerations once residence is granted.

Your next step

If you are searching for a Spanish immigration lawyer, look beyond whether someone can file. Ask whether they can diagnose the case, structure it properly, and connect immigration with tax, timing and long-term residence planning.

That is where many applicants lose time. They are eligible on paper, but the file is weak in execution, and once an administrative defect has been recorded against the file, it is rarely corrected without delay.

Many people can qualify for residence in Spain and still face delay or refusal because the route was poorly chosen, the tax implications were ignored, or the documentation was not presented strategically.

The key question is not whether you meet the requirements on paper, but whether your case can withstand administrative scrutiny under a system that, in 2026, is more interconnected than ever. Most errors at this stage cannot be corrected afterwards without losing time, optionality or the special regime altogether.

Legal Fournier advises on Spanish immigration and tax matters as one coordinated process, so applicants can evaluate the right path before committing time and money to the wrong one.

Whichever profile fits, the diagnosis runs first.

Digital nomad with family relocating together — coordinating the visa, the special inbound regime and the schooling timeline.

Senior executive on an intra-corporate transfer — aligning the employer’s payroll structure with the residence pathway and Beckham eligibility.

Investor or entrepreneur structuring a Spanish base — mapping a residence pathway onto a corporate, tax and Social Security structure that is internally consistent.

Company relocating talent into Spain — managing multiple files in parallel without exposing the group to inconsistent positions across employees.

In every case, the underlying question is the same: does the file survive scrutiny under the immigration and tax rules that apply on the date of filing?

Every case involves specific facts and circumstances that may affect the outcome under the LO 4/2000, the Real Decreto 1155/2024, the Ley 28/2022, the Ley 35/2006 del IRPF and the Ley 39/2015 of administrative procedure. documents.title: Open a Company in Spain: A Strategic Guide for Foreigners
documents.description: You are probably at the stage where Spain looks straightforward on paper. The market is chosen, the offering is defined, and most online guides suggest that to open a company in Spain you only need a few forms, a notary appointment, and a bank account. In practice, that is where many foreign founders lose time. […]
documents.text:
You are probably at the stage where Spain looks straightforward on paper. The market is chosen, the offering is defined, and most online guides suggest that to open a company in Spain you only need a few forms, a notary appointment, and a bank account.

In practice, that is where many foreign founders lose time. We regularly see applicants with a sound business idea but a weak legal setup: the wrong corporate form, a power of attorney that the notary will not accept, bylaws that do not match the actual activity, or post-incorporation obligations treated as an afterthought. Spain does allow entry at very low capital thresholds after the reform of article 4 LSC by Ley 18/2022 (Crea y Crece) (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2022-15818), but a low cost of formation does not translate into a low cost of mistakes.

The Reality of Starting a Business in Spain

A typical foreign founder who decides to open a company in Spain arrives with urgency. They want to invoice quickly, secure a lease, hire one person, or apply for residency linked to the business. The incorporation file is only part of the problem. The Spanish authorities and the bank cross-check shareholder identity, corporate purpose, tax registration, and sector-specific permissions before anything moves, and they do not flag inconsistencies in advance. The file simply stops at the notary, at the bank, or at the Registro Mercantil. We see this monthly.

Spain has positioned itself as accessible for foreign capital (see ICEX-Invest in Spain (https://www.investinspain.org/) for the official policy framing), and the Sociedad Limitada (SL) can now be incorporated with as little as €1 after Ley 18/2022. The fine print is what most guides skip: while paid-in capital remains below €3,000, at least 20% of profit must be allocated to legal reserve until the threshold is reached, and shareholders respond jointly and severally for the difference between €3,000 and the subscribed capital if the company is liquidated insolvent. A €1 SL is technically possible. In front of a Spanish bank or a serious counterparty, it almost never reads well.

A company can be legally formed and still be poorly structured for the business it is meant to run.

Choosing Your Legal Structure: A Foundational Decision

The first serious decision the founder makes is structural rather than procedural. Founders often treat the legal form as a filing choice (https://legalfournier.com/en/business-in-spain/eu-inc-28th-regime-company-formation/), when in fact it shapes liability under article 1911 of the Código Civil, governance, tax treatment, profit extraction, and, for many international founders in 2026, the personal tax position under the displaced-workers regime.

Why the structure affects more than setup

For foreign entrepreneurs, the Sociedad Limitada is often the right vehicle, but not automatically. A sole-trader (autónomo) setup may appear simpler, yet personal liability under article 1911 of the Código Civil and the activity-based contribution regime introduced by Real Decreto-ley 13/2022 can become uncomfortable very quickly. A branch (sucursal) can work for an established foreign group, but many parents underestimate how Spanish exposure flows back to the head office for compliance and litigation purposes. An SL, by contrast, can give a clear separation between business and personal assets, but only if the bylaws and the administrator’s role are designed for what the company will actually do.

A useful starting point is to review the legal framework around forming a Spanish limited company (https://legalfournier.com/en/business-in-spain/constitucion-de-la-sociedad-limitada/), then assess whether that structure fits the ownership model and the operating plan. Founders who plan to relocate should also read this together with the Entrepreneur Visa (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/entrepreneur-visa/) framework, because corporate and immigration files reinforce each other.

The Beckham regime: where the corporate structure becomes a personal tax decision

For most international founders relocating to Spain in 2026, the SL is set up precisely so the founder can become an employee or qualifying administrator of their own Spanish company and apply for the displaced-workers regime under article 93 LIRPF, the so-called Beckham regime, which applies a flat 24% rate on employment income up to €600,000. The regime is generous, yet not granted to a generic SL. Eligibility is conditioned by the relationship between founder and company, the shareholding percentages, the way remuneration is structured, and the timing of the application before the Agencia Tributaria. An SL opened “the cheap way” can quietly disqualify the founder from one of the most valuable personal tax benefits in the EU, and the loss is rarely reversible once the application has been filed.

What we look at in practice

When we advise on structure, the question is rarely “what is cheapest to open?”. It is closer to this:

Residency position. Will the founder live in Spain, manage remotely, or relocate later? Tax residency under article 9 LIRPF interacts with the corporate vehicle and the Beckham application.

Control mechanics. Multiple shareholders, uneven contributions, future investors, vesting, drag-along: the LSC defaults are not always optimal, which is where customised bylaws and a shareholders’ agreement do the real work.

Payment strategy. Salary, dividends, or reinvested revenue each carry a different tax and Social Security profile, and each interacts with the Beckham eligibility differently.

Risk profile. Regulated, client-facing, or contract-heavy activities require a stronger corporate presentation than a generic incorporation can provide.

Practical rule. If the structure only works for the first month, it is the wrong structure.

Navigating the Administrative Gauntlet: NIE, Bank Accounts and Notaries

Most files that fail do not collapse because the founder lacks motivation. They fail because one dependency blocks the next. For non-residents, the process is exposed to document quality, sequencing, and representation issues that only become visible when something stops moving.

Why these files break as a system, not as a checklist

Foreign incorporations rarely fail at one specific step. They fail because three different blocks have to be designed together, and the seams between them are where the file actually breaks. None of the three blocks is solved in isolation by ticking items off a list.

Three blocks that have to hold together

Personal capacity in Spain. Founder and administrator have to be visible, identifiable, and able to sign in a way the Spanish system recognises. When this block is wrong, every later step inherits the defect.

The notarial act. Corporate purpose, capital, bylaws, identification, and representation have to align inside a single deed. Most files that collapse here collapse silently, with no advance warning from the notary or the bank.

Post-formation reality. Tax, Social Security, foreign-investment reporting and ongoing compliance start immediately after the deed and decide whether the SL actually works as a vehicle.

In our practice, files break less often inside one of the three blocks than at the seams between them. That is the layer a founder cannot debug from the outside.

Where non-residents get stuck

The two recurring stop-points are the NIE and the bank. A founder without a Spanish tax identifier cannot subscribe shares, sign the deed, or open the corporate account. Where the founder cannot travel to Spain, we obtain the NIE (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/nie-number/) through the appropriate remote channel under the Hague Convention of 1961 framework; the work is straightforward when the file is properly drafted and is the most common reason a non-resident incorporation fails when it is not. The same logic applies to the deed itself, where our apostille and document legalization (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/apostille-services/) service is usually the silent gating item.

On the banking side, customer-due-diligence under Ley 10/2010 has hardened. Spanish banks are slow with non-resident shareholders precisely because their compliance teams are screening the structure, not the founder’s intent. We pre-validate the corporate structure with the bank’s compliance department before the in-branch appointment, because that is where most non-resident files actually fail. Our overview of opening a bank account in Spain for foreigners and businesses (https://legalfournier.com/en/tax-finance/opening-a-bank-account-in-spain/) explains why banks often become the first real bottleneck.

What the notary actually controls, and the trap of template bylaws

The notary controls the legality of the deed of incorporation and the Registro Mercantil performs a second qualification. If shareholder identity, corporate purpose, capital evidence, or the bylaws are inconsistent, the signing is delayed or refused. Three pressure points come up repeatedly:

Name reservation issues. A preferred denomination may be rejected, which creates delay if alternatives were not prepared.

Banking mismatch. The bank asks for one set of documents, while the notary expects another sequence; founders without local representation often discover the gap mid-process.

Template bylaws used as default. The fast-track platforms (including the public CIRCE / PAE electronic gateway (https://paeelectronico.es/)) incorporate with standard estatutos that lack pactos de socios, share-transfer regimes, remote-work clauses, and tailored governance. Twelve months later, the saved week becomes a structural block when investors, founder exits, or licensing partners ask for governance language the template never contemplated.

A boutique firm earns its place by incorporating once, with bylaws built to survive the first round of complexity, rather than by racing a public platform to a same-week deed.

Common and Costly Mistakes in Company Formation

The errors we see most often look harmless at the moment they happen. The cost shows up months later, when they have already affected credibility, tax treatment, or the administrative file. The Spanish market is competitive, and administrative delay carries a commercial cost even when the underlying business is sound.

The mistakes we see most often

Undercapitalisation. The legal minimum and a sensible operating capital are not the same thing. A €1 incorporation may save days at the notary and lose weeks at the bank.

Corporate purpose drafted badly. If the bylaws describe one activity and the company invoices another, tax census and IAE classification problems follow.

Weak registered-office strategy. A temporary or poorly chosen domicilio social creates notice problems for AEAT and Seguridad Social and erodes credibility with counterparties.

Failing to register the trademark with the OEPM. The Registro Mercantil controls the corporate denomination, not the brand. A registered trademark at the Oficina Española de Patentes y Marcas (https://www.oepm.es/) can block the commercial use of a name even when the SL is properly incorporated. The two filings should be coordinated, not sequential.

Treating formation as the end point. Many founders organise the incorporation carefully and then go quiet for the next quarter, which is exactly when the real compliance machine starts running.

A neat checklist will not protect you from a file that makes legal sense in one country but not in Spain.

The Work Begins After Incorporation: Ongoing Compliance

Once the company exists, the risk profile shifts from delay to penalty. The Ley General Tributaria automates a meaningful share of the exposure: article 198 fixes minimum penalties for late or zero-debt filings, and article 191 imposes penalties of 50% to 150% of any undeclared tax debt. The pressure is structural, not anecdotal, and a quiet first year of compliance failures often becomes the most expensive part of the founder’s first three years in Spain.

What founders tend to underestimate

After incorporation, several obligations arrive quickly and they are not optional:

Tax census registration. The Modelo 036 filed at the AEAT electronic office (https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/) must reflect the real activity, the VAT position, and the IAE epigraph, and it must match what the bylaws say the company does.

Administrator and Social Security regime. The administrator’s enrolment in the relevant Tesorería General de la Seguridad Social (https://www.seg-social.es/) scheme cannot be deferred without consequences; the rules tightened with Real Decreto-ley 13/2022.

Foreign-investment declaration. Where shareholders are non-resident, the declaration before the Registro de Inversiones Exteriores is often overlooked entirely.

Beneficial-ownership and ongoing filings. Quarterly and annual obligations, plus titularidad real reporting, continue whether the company is active, slow, or still organising itself.

The personal liability the SL does not protect against

Foreign founders often assume that an SL means absolute limitation of liability. It does not. Article 367 LSC imposes joint and several liability on administrators for company obligations arising after a cause of dissolution materialises (typically losses below half of the share capital) if the administrator does not call the shareholders’ meeting within two months. Article 43 of the Ley General Tributaria adds subsidiary administrator liability for unpaid tax debts where negligence or breach of duties is established. The corporate ring-fence works, on condition that the formal duties are kept current. In that sense, monthly accounting and tax compliance function as patrimonial protection more than as bookkeeping, and they are what keeps the founder’s personal patrimony outside the company’s risk perimeter. Services such as monthly accounting and tax compliance in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/monthly-accounting/) are most useful when the founder does not speak Spanish, manages remotely, or needs filings to align with a residence or tax planning position.

A company is formed in a single notarial act, and then proven again every quarter.

What It Really Takes to Open a Company in Spain

Spain’s system is not impossible to navigate, but it punishes casual assumptions. The legal path to open a company in Spain depends on who the founders are, where they sign, how they are represented, what the company will do, and whether immigration or tax planning sits behind the incorporation. Two files with the same SL on paper can have very different real exposures.

When legal advice is the better economic decision

A strategic review is recommended where any of the following apply:

You are a non-resident founder and want to incorporate without travelling repeatedly.

The shareholding is not simple, especially where family members, investors, or a foreign parent company are involved.

You may relocate to Spain and want to preserve eligibility for the Beckham regime under article 93 LIRPF.

The business is regulated or licensed, even when generic guides make it sound otherwise.

You need the company operational quickly, because speed without legal coherence usually creates more delay, not less.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a foreigner open a company in Spain without residency?

Yes. Spanish corporate law does not require residency to be a shareholder or, in most cases, to be the administrator of an SL. The constraints are practical: a Spanish tax identifier, an apostilled power of attorney where the deed is signed remotely, and a banking counterparty willing to onboard a non-resident structure. What stops these files is rarely the corporate law side. It is usually the bank, working backwards from its KYC review, and we routinely see clean incorporations sit for six weeks waiting for a Spanish account that should have been pre-validated weeks earlier.

What is the minimum capital required after Ley 18/2022?

Article 4 of the Texto Refundido de la Ley de Sociedades de Capital, as modified by Ley 18/2022, sets the minimum at €1 for a Sociedad Limitada. Until paid-in capital reaches €3,000, at least 20% of the year’s profit must go to legal reserve, and shareholders are jointly and severally liable for the difference between the subscribed capital and €3,000 if the company is liquidated insolvent. In practice, banks and counterparties read a €1 SL as undercapitalised even when it is technically lawful. The real question for a foreign founder is whether they want to spend the first year explaining a decision that saved a few euros at incorporation.

Can a foreign founder qualify for the Beckham regime through a Spanish SL?

Possibly. Article 93 LIRPF allows displaced workers to apply a flat 24% rate on employment income up to €600,000, and recent reforms have extended the regime to certain founders and qualifying administrators of Spanish entities. Eligibility is conditioned by the relationship between the founder and the company, the shareholding percentage, the source of remuneration, and the timing of the application. We have seen the regime denied for SLs that were structurally clean on paper but where the administrator’s contract or the participation percentage was set without the Beckham rules in mind. After a denial, the alternative routes narrow considerably.

Can I sign the deed remotely if I cannot travel to Spain?

In principle, yes. A power of attorney executed before a notary in your home country and apostilled under the Hague Convention of 1961 can authorise a representative to subscribe shares and sign the deed in Spain. The risk lies in the wording: a generic POA is rarely enough, and even a tailored one can be rejected if the scope, capacity, or formal requirements diverge from what the Spanish notary or bank expects.

Is the incorporation itself the main legal risk for a foreign founder?

Usually not. Most of what we end up rescuing for foreign clients started before the deed was signed, in how the file was assembled, or after it was registered, in how the first compliance year was run. The incorporation deed itself is the visible part of the process, and rarely the part where damage actually happens.

documents.title: Residencia de larga duración en España: guía de solicitud
documents.description: La residencia de larga duración en España no es una simple renovación de la tarjeta que ya tiene el extranjero. Es una autorización distinta, con efectos más estables y con un examen propio por parte de la Oficina de Extranjería. Bajo el artículo 32 de la Ley Orgánica 4/2000 y el Reglamento de Extranjería aprobado […]
documents.text:
La residencia de larga duración en España no es una simple renovación de la tarjeta que ya tiene el extranjero. Es una autorización distinta, con efectos más estables y con un examen propio por parte de la Oficina de Extranjería. Bajo el artículo 32 de la Ley Orgánica 4/2000 y el Reglamento de Extranjería aprobado por el Real Decreto 1155/2024, vigente desde el 20 de mayo de 2025, la Administración no se limita a comprobar que han pasado cinco años. Revisa si esos años cuentan, si la residencia fue legal y continuada, si las ausencias están dentro de los límites, si la documentación extranjera es válida y si la vía elegida encaja con la realidad del expediente.

El error habitual es preparar la solicitud como si fuera una renovación más. En nuestra experiencia, esa lectura crea problemas. Una renovación puede superar pequeñas inconsistencias si el permiso anterior sigue una línea clara. La autorización de larga duración exige algo más: una reconstrucción completa del historial de residencia, viajes, autorizaciones anteriores, antecedentes penales y, cuando se solicita la modalidad UE, recursos económicos y seguro médico con un estándar más alto. Antes de presentar, conviene revisar también la posición de renovación de residencia (https://legalfournier.com/es/servicio/renovacion-residencia/) y la tasa de solicitud mediante el Modelo 790 código 052 (https://sede.administracionespublicas.gob.es/pagina/index/directorio/tasa052), epígrafe 2.6.

Actualizado: 11 de mayo de 2026. Contenido alineado con el Real Decreto 1155/2024.

Puntos clave antes de presentar

Regla general. Cinco años de residencia legal y continuada en España, salvo las vías alternativas reconocidas por el artículo 32.2 LOEX.

Continuidad. Las ausencias no deben superar seis meses seguidos ni diez meses en total dentro del periodo de cinco años. Si se justifican por actividad laboral o profesional debidamente comunicada, el margen puede llegar a doce meses.

Nacional o UE. La residencia de larga duración nacional suele ser más defendible cuando los recursos o el seguro no son perfectamente regulares. La modalidad UE exige más prueba, pero ofrece movilidad en otros Estados miembros.

Riesgos frecuentes. Ausencias mal calculadas, antecedentes mal legalizados, categoría incorrecta, seguro insuficiente, recursos económicos mal acreditados o retrasos en la TIE después de la concesión.

Plazo de resolución. Tres meses. El silencio administrativo puede operar en sentido positivo, pero no sustituye la obtención material de la tarjeta.

La larga duración es una autorización nueva, no una renovación

En una renovación ordinaria, la Oficina de Extranjería comprueba si el extranjero mantiene las condiciones de su autorización previa. En la residencia larga duracion espana, el análisis cambia. La Administración valora si el extranjero puede acceder a un estatus indefinido, con derechos amplios de residencia y trabajo. Eso implica revisar el historial completo, no solo la tarjeta actual.

El expediente debe demostrar una línea coherente de residencia legal. Si hubo cambios de permiso, periodos de estudio, autorizaciones vinculadas a trabajo remoto, estancias por formación, modificaciones de régimen o periodos con documentación débil, esos tramos deben explicarse antes de presentar. Esperar a que la Oficina los detecte mediante un requerimiento suele dejar poco margen para corregir.

No basta con entregar muchos documentos. La solicitud debe contar una historia jurídica coherente: qué autorización tuvo el cliente en cada periodo, por qué ese periodo computa y cómo se mantiene la continuidad.

Residencia de larga duración nacional o residencia de larga duración UE

La primera decisión técnica consiste en elegir entre la autorización nacional y la autorización de larga duración UE. Ambas se apoyan en el periodo de cinco años, pero no tienen la misma carga probatoria ni los mismos efectos. La modalidad nacional permite residir y trabajar en España con carácter indefinido. La modalidad UE añade ventajas de movilidad en otros Estados miembros, de acuerdo con la Directiva 2003/109/CE, pero exige recursos estables y regulares y seguro público o privado con cobertura equivalente al Sistema Nacional de Salud.

| Criterio
| Larga duración nacional
| Larga duración UE

| Base principal
| Cinco años de residencia legal y continuada
| Cinco años de residencia legal y continuada

| Recursos económicos
| Control contextual, menos intenso
| Recursos estables, regulares y suficientes

| Seguro médico
| Cobertura adecuada según el caso
| Cobertura equivalente al sistema público

| Movilidad europea
| Limitada al marco español
| Más útil si el cliente quiere trasladarse a otro Estado miembro

| Perfil de riesgo
| Más sólido cuando la economía del cliente es variable
| Más vulnerable si los recursos o el seguro parecen preparados a última hora

La autorización más ambiciosa no siempre es la más inteligente. Un autónomo con ingresos altos pero irregulares, un fundador que cobra de varias sociedades o una familia con seguro privado lleno de exclusiones puede tener una solicitud nacional fuerte y una solicitud UE débil. La estrategia no debe partir del nombre del permiso, sino de lo que los documentos ya pueden defender.

La regla de continuidad de cinco años

El requisito central es haber residido legalmente y de forma continuada durante cinco años. La palabra clave es “continuada”. La residencia no se calcula por intuición, por recuerdos de viajes o por la fecha en que el cliente siente que se instaló en España. Se calcula a partir de autorizaciones, pasaportes, entradas y salidas, certificados, empadronamiento, resoluciones anteriores y demás documentación administrativa.

Las ausencias de hasta seis meses seguidos no rompen la continuidad si el total de ausencias dentro de los cinco años no supera diez meses. Cuando las salidas se vinculan a actividad laboral, profesional o no lucrativa debidamente comunicada, el margen puede llegar a doce meses. Esa excepción no debe tratarse como automática. Hay que probar por qué el viaje se produjo, cómo se relaciona con la actividad y si fue comunicado o puede documentarse con suficiente fuerza.

Errores habituales al calcular ausencias

Contar de memoria. Los viajes cortos se olvidan, especialmente en perfiles de negocio o trabajo remoto.

Mirar solo cada salida aislada. El problema suele estar en el acumulado, no en un viaje concreto.

Presuponer que todo viaje de trabajo está protegido. La causa profesional necesita soporte documental.

Ignorar periodos que computan parcialmente. Estudios, formación, movilidad o prácticas pueden requerir un análisis distinto.

Cuando el historial está cerca del límite, la fecha de presentación se convierte en una decisión jurídica. A veces lo correcto es esperar, recuperar margen de continuidad y presentar después. Presentar rápido con una línea temporal débil puede convertir un expediente defendible en una denegación evitable.

Vías alternativas fuera del recorrido de cinco años

El artículo 32.2 LOEX reconoce situaciones que no encajan exactamente en el camino ordinario de cinco años. Pueden acceder, si cumplen los requisitos específicos, personas nacidas en España que al alcanzar la mayoría de edad hayan residido legal y continuadamente durante los tres años anteriores a la solicitud; antiguos españoles que perdieron la nacionalidad; y beneficiarios de protección subsidiaria en los términos previstos por la normativa.

Estas vías no son atajos. Cada una exige una narrativa jurídica propia. Un antiguo nacional español no prueba su caso igual que una persona nacida en España. Un beneficiario de protección subsidiaria necesita acreditar la protección y su continuidad. El fallo habitual es identificar la vía correcta y preparar después un expediente genérico como si se tratara de la residencia ordinaria de cinco años.

Documentos: dónde suelen fallar las solicitudes

Muchos expedientes denegados parecen completos a primera vista. El problema no es que falte papel. El problema es que el documento aportado no cumple la función jurídica que debe cumplir.

Antecedentes penales extranjeros. El certificado existe, pero está caducado, mal apostillado, legalizado por una vía incorrecta o traducido fuera del marco de traducción jurada exigible.

Pasaporte. Se aporta copia, pero nadie ha reconciliado los sellos y viajes con el argumento de continuidad.

Historial de permisos. La tarjeta actual está vigente, pero la cadena de autorizaciones anteriores no está claramente documentada.

Recursos para la modalidad UE. Hay dinero, pero no se demuestra estabilidad y regularidad a lo largo del tiempo.

Seguro médico. Existe una póliza privada, pero contiene copagos, carencias o exclusiones que pueden ser problemáticas en el expediente UE.

También conviene revisar la tasa. Un pago correcto no salva un expediente débil, pero un pago incorrecto puede crear un requerimiento innecesario y retrasar el caso. En solicitudes de larga duración, cada detalle administrativo debe acompañar a la teoría jurídica del expediente.

Plazos, silencio administrativo y fase de TIE

La solicitud puede presentarse dentro de los sesenta días previos a la caducidad de la autorización actual y, con posible exposición sancionadora, dentro de los noventa días posteriores. Esa ventana no elimina la necesidad de cumplir el requisito material de cinco años, pero sí afecta a la estrategia cuando la tarjeta está cerca de caducar o cuando hay ausencias que presionan el cálculo de continuidad.

El plazo de resolución es de tres meses. Si no hay resolución expresa, el silencio administrativo opera de forma favorable conforme a la disposición adicional primera de la LOEX. Aun así, el silencio positivo no entrega físicamente la tarjeta. Hay que acreditar la situación, impulsar la emisión y solicitar la TIE dentro del cauce correcto. En esta fase, la gestión de la cita TIE (https://legalfournier.com/es/inmigracion/citas-tie-2026-como-conseguir-cita-evitar-errores/) deja de ser un trámite menor y pasa a formar parte de la conservación práctica del derecho obtenido.

Muchas complicaciones aparecen después de una resolución favorable. El cliente gana el expediente, pero no solicita la tarjeta a tiempo, no documenta intentos de cita o deja pasar plazos porque confunde aprobación con cierre definitivo. La autorización puede ser indefinida, pero la ejecución administrativa sigue teniendo fechas y pruebas.

Diferencias entre Oficinas de Extranjería

La norma es estatal, pero la práctica no siempre es uniforme. Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Alicante, Málaga u oficinas más pequeñas pueden aplicar criterios internos distintos sobre continuidad, ausencias por trabajo, suficiencia de recursos o prueba del seguro. La guía ministerial fija el marco general, pero la forma en que cada oficina examina el expediente puede variar.

Esto importa especialmente cuando el cliente se ha movido entre provincias durante los cinco años. La oficina competente, el padrón, la tarjeta, los cambios de domicilio y los antecedentes administrativos deben cuadrar. Un expediente preparado para una provincia no siempre se defiende igual en otra.

Derechos después de la concesión

La residencia de larga duración permite residir y trabajar en España con carácter indefinido. El titular no está renovando periódicamente el derecho de residencia en sentido sustantivo, sino la tarjeta física que lo documenta. Esa distinción es importante para clientes que piensan que la caducidad de la TIE equivale a la pérdida automática del estatus.

La concesión también suele tener consecuencias fiscales y de planificación familiar o empresarial. Para clientes internacionales, la larga duración confirma que España ha dejado de ser una estancia temporal y se ha convertido en centro de vida. En ese momento conviene alinear residencia, fiscalidad, patrimonio, sociedades y planificación familiar antes de que aparezcan problemas de cumplimiento.

Denegación y recursos

Una denegación puede deberse a ausencias mal calculadas, categoría equivocada, antecedentes mal legalizados, recursos insuficientes, seguro inadecuado o errores posteriores a la aprobación. Algunas denegaciones son difíciles de evitar. Muchas no lo son si el expediente se revisa antes.

Frente a una resolución negativa, normalmente existe un mes para presentar recurso potestativo de reposición y dos meses para acudir a la vía contencioso-administrativa. Perder esos plazos convierte el problema en algo mucho más serio: la resolución gana firmeza y el cliente puede quedar obligado a reconstruir su estrategia desde la autorización anterior, si todavía es viable.

El recurso no debe redactarse como una simple queja. Debe atacar el motivo concreto de la denegación, aportar la prueba que faltaba si procesalmente es admisible y explicar por qué la interpretación de la Oficina no se sostiene con la normativa aplicable. En casos de continuidad dudosa, el recurso exige un trabajo detallado de línea temporal.

Cuándo conviene una revisión legal antes de presentar

La asistencia legal es especialmente recomendable cuando el cliente tiene viajes frecuentes, ingresos variables, sociedades en varios países, intención de solicitar la modalidad UE, antecedentes administrativos, una denegación previa o una familia dependiente que también debe computar continuidad. En esos supuestos, el trabajo no consiste en rellenar un formulario. Consiste en decidir qué vía se defiende mejor, cuándo conviene presentar y qué documentos deben producirse para anticipar objeciones.

También vemos riesgo en perfiles que han pasado por varias figuras migratorias: estudiante, prácticas, teletrabajo internacional, residencia no lucrativa, cuenta propia, arraigo o familiar comunitario. Cada transición puede afectar al cálculo y a la forma de presentar la solicitud. Un expediente con muchas piezas no es necesariamente débil, pero sí necesita orden técnico.

Preguntas frecuentes sobre residencia de larga duración en España

¿Quién puede solicitar la residencia de larga duración en España?

La regla general exige cinco años de residencia legal y continuada. También existen vías específicas para personas nacidas en España que cumplen los requisitos de residencia previa, antiguos españoles que perdieron la nacionalidad y beneficiarios de protección subsidiaria. En todos los casos, la viabilidad real depende de revisar el historial documental completo.

¿Las ausencias pueden romper la continuidad?

Sí. La continuidad admite ausencias de hasta seis meses seguidos y diez meses en total dentro del periodo de cinco años. En ciertos supuestos vinculados a actividad laboral o profesional, el margen puede llegar a doce meses, pero debe estar documentado. Si el expediente depende de esa excepción, conviene revisarlo antes de presentar.

¿Qué diferencia hay entre la larga duración nacional y la UE?

La nacional consolida la residencia indefinida en España. La UE puede facilitar movilidad en otros Estados miembros, pero exige más prueba sobre recursos y seguro. La decisión correcta depende del perfil documental del cliente, no solo del beneficio teórico de la modalidad UE.

¿La residencia de larga duración caduca?

El estatus es indefinido, pero la TIE física debe renovarse periódicamente. La renovación de la tarjeta no equivale a solicitar de nuevo la autorización, aunque las ausencias prolongadas o ciertos problemas posteriores pueden afectar al estatus.

¿Pueden denegar la solicitud aunque haya vivido cinco años en España?

Sí. Los cinco años son condición necesaria, pero no garantizan la concesión. La Oficina revisa continuidad, legalidad de la residencia, antecedentes, documentación y adecuación de la vía elegida. Por eso la auditoría previa del expediente suele ser más importante que la propia presentación.

Conclusión: revise el expediente antes de solicitar

La residencia de larga duración en España es un hito importante, pero no debe tratarse como un trámite automático. El expediente debe demostrar continuidad, legalidad, coherencia documental y una elección correcta entre la vía nacional y la vía UE. Cuando el cliente tiene ausencias, ingresos variables, cambios de permiso o documentación extranjera compleja, la diferencia entre concesión y denegación suele decidirse antes de presentar.

En Legal Fournier revisamos expedientes de larga duración desde una perspectiva legal y estratégica: ruta adecuada, cálculo de ausencias, documentación extranjera, prueba económica, riesgos por provincia y fase posterior de TIE.

Aviso legal. Este artículo tiene carácter informativo y no constituye asesoramiento jurídico. La aplicación del artículo 32 LOEX y del Real Decreto 1155/2024 depende de los hechos concretos de cada expediente y del criterio de la Oficina de Extranjería competente.

Cuéntenos su caso (https://legalfournier.com/es/contacto/)

documents.text:
La résidence de longue durée en Espagne est souvent présentée comme la suite naturelle de cinq années de séjour légal. Cette lecture est trop simple. En droit espagnol, il ne s’agit pas d’un renouvellement ordinaire de carte, mais d’une autorisation autonome, évaluée selon ses propres critères. L’article 32 de la Loi organique 4/2000 et le Règlement des étrangers approuvé par le Real Decreto 1155/2024, en vigueur depuis le 20 mai 2025, imposent une analyse complète de la continuité, des absences, des autorisations antérieures, des antécédents pénaux et, pour la modalité UE, de la stabilité économique et de l’assurance médicale.

Dans la pratique, le risque vient rarement d’un formulaire mal rempli. Il vient plutôt d’un dossier qui n’a pas été reconstruit avant le dépôt. Un client peut avoir vécu en Espagne pendant cinq ans et rester vulnérable si une période ne compte pas, si des voyages répétés dépassent les limites admises, si un certificat étranger n’est pas correctement légalisé ou si la voie UE est choisie alors que les revenus ou l’assurance ne résistent pas à l’examen administratif.

Mis à jour : 11 mai 2026. Analyse alignée sur le Real Decreto 1155/2024.

Points essentiels

Règle générale. Cinq ans de résidence légale et continue en Espagne, sauf cas particuliers reconnus par l’article 32.2 LOEX.

Continuité. Les absences ne doivent pas dépasser six mois consécutifs ni dix mois au total sur cinq ans. Dans certains cas professionnels documentés, le plafond peut atteindre douze mois.

Voie nationale ou voie UE. La voie nationale est souvent plus défendable lorsque les revenus ou l’assurance ne sont pas parfaitement réguliers. La voie UE offre une mobilité plus large, mais exige davantage de preuves.

Motifs fréquents de refus. Absences mal calculées, documents étrangers défectueux, catégorie mal choisie, assurance insuffisante, ressources mal prouvées ou mauvaise gestion de la TIE après accord.

Délai de décision. Trois mois. Le silence administratif peut être positif, mais il ne remplace pas l’obtention matérielle de la carte.

Une autorisation distincte, pas une simple prolongation

Lors d’un renouvellement classique, l’administration vérifie si les conditions du permis précédent restent remplies. Pour la résidence permanente Espagne, l’analyse est différente. L’Oficina de Extranjería examine si les faits permettent d’accorder un statut indéfini avec des droits étendus de résidence et de travail. Cela suppose une lecture complète du parcours migratoire.

Il faut donc éviter de réutiliser le dossier de la dernière carte comme modèle. Les autorisations précédentes ne créent pas un droit automatique à la longue durée. Le dossier doit expliquer chaque période : type d’autorisation, dates de validité, changements de statut, voyages, éventuelles périodes d’études ou de formation, et lien entre tous ces éléments. Lorsque l’historique est complexe, le travail commence souvent par l’audit de la dernière renouvellement de résidence (https://legalfournier.com/fr/service/renouvellement-residence/) et par la vérification des taxes liées au dossier.

Un dossier volumineux n’est pas forcément un dossier solide. Les preuves doivent soutenir une théorie juridique claire : pourquoi le client remplit la condition de durée, pourquoi la continuité n’est pas rompue et pourquoi la voie choisie est la bonne.

Résidence longue durée nationale ou résidence longue durée UE

La première décision stratégique consiste à choisir entre la résidence de longue durée nationale et la résidence de longue durée UE. Les deux reposent sur une base commune de cinq années de résidence légale et continue. La différence tient aux effets et à la charge de preuve. La voie nationale consolide la situation en Espagne. La voie UE, issue de la directive 2003/109/CE, peut faciliter une mobilité ultérieure dans d’autres États membres, mais elle exige des ressources stables et régulières ainsi qu’une assurance médicale publique ou privée comparable à la couverture du système national de santé.

| Critère
| Longue durée nationale
| Longue durée UE

| Base principale
| Cinq ans de résidence légale et continue
| Cinq ans de résidence légale et continue

| Ressources
| Contrôle plus contextuel
| Ressources stables, régulières et suffisantes

| Assurance médicale
| Couverture adaptée au cas
| Couverture équivalente au système public

| Mobilité dans l’UE
| Effet principalement espagnol
| Plus utile si un transfert vers un autre État membre est envisagé

| Profil de risque
| Souvent plus solide lorsque les revenus sont variables
| Plus fragile si la preuve économique semble récente ou insuffisante

La voie la plus ambitieuse n’est donc pas toujours la meilleure. Un indépendant avec des revenus élevés mais irréguliers, un fondateur payé par plusieurs sociétés ou une famille disposant d’une assurance privée avec exclusions peut avoir un bon dossier national et un dossier UE vulnérable. La décision doit partir des preuves disponibles, pas du nom du permis.

La règle des cinq années de continuité

La condition de cinq ans semble simple. Elle ne l’est pas toujours. La résidence doit être légale et continue. L’administration ne compte pas selon le souvenir du client, mais à partir des autorisations, du passeport, des tampons d’entrée et de sortie, des résolutions, du padrón, des certificats et de l’ensemble des données disponibles.

Les absences inférieures à six mois consécutifs ne rompent pas la continuité si le total sur cinq ans ne dépasse pas dix mois. Lorsque les absences sont liées à une activité professionnelle ou non lucrative dûment communiquée et documentée, elles peuvent être admises jusqu’à douze mois au total. Cette exception doit être préparée avec prudence. Il ne suffit pas d’affirmer que le voyage était professionnel : il faut le prouver et l’intégrer dans la chronologie du dossier.

Les erreurs de calcul les plus fréquentes

Compter de mémoire. Les voyages courts sont souvent oubliés, surtout chez les cadres, consultants et travailleurs à distance.

Ignorer le total cumulé. Chaque voyage peut sembler mineur, mais l’addition peut dépasser le seuil.

Supposer que tout déplacement professionnel est protégé. La cause professionnelle doit être documentée et cohérente avec l’activité du client.

Mal traiter les périodes particulières. Études, formation, mobilité ou stages peuvent nécessiter un calcul distinct.

Lorsque le dossier se situe près des limites, la date de dépôt devient une décision juridique. Dans certains cas, attendre quelques mois permet de reconstituer une marge de continuité et d’éviter une demande fragile. Déposer vite n’est pas toujours déposer mieux.

Les voies alternatives reconnues par la loi

La voie ordinaire repose sur cinq années de résidence. Elle n’est pas la seule. L’article 32.2 LOEX reconnaît aussi des situations particulières : personnes nées en Espagne qui, à leur majorité, ont résidé légalement et continûment pendant les trois années précédant la demande ; anciens ressortissants espagnols ayant perdu la nationalité ; bénéficiaires de protection subsidiaire lorsque les conditions spécifiques sont remplies.

Ces voies sont utiles, mais elles ne sont pas des raccourcis. Chacune exige une preuve différente. Un ancien Espagnol doit documenter l’acquisition et la perte de nationalité. Une personne née en Espagne doit prouver la résidence légale des années pertinentes. Un bénéficiaire de protection subsidiaire doit rattacher le statut de protection au parcours de résidence. Le dossier doit donc être construit autour de la bonne base légale.

Documents : pourquoi un dossier complet peut rester faible

Beaucoup de refus portent sur des documents qui semblaient corrects au client. Le certificat existe, mais il n’est plus valable. La traduction existe, mais elle n’est pas assermentée. Le passeport est joint, mais les voyages qu’il révèle contredisent la continuité annoncée. Les relevés bancaires montrent des fonds, mais pas la stabilité requise pour la voie UE.

Casier judiciaire étranger. Il doit être obtenu dans le bon pays, dans le bon délai, avec légalisation ou apostille et traduction adaptée.

Passeport et voyages. Les entrées et sorties doivent correspondre à la chronologie présentée.

Historique de permis. Les changements de statut doivent être expliqués, surtout si certains périodes ne comptent pas pleinement.

Preuve économique. Pour la voie UE, la régularité des ressources compte autant que le montant.

Assurance médicale. Une police privée peut être insuffisante si elle contient des exclusions importantes, copaiements ou délais de carence.

La taxe administrative doit également être correcte. Une erreur dans le paiement ne détermine pas seule le fond du dossier, mais elle peut générer un requerimiento inutile et retarder une demande déjà sensible au calendrier.

Délais, silence administratif et carte TIE

La demande peut être déposée pendant les soixante jours précédant l’expiration de l’autorisation en cours et, avec un risque de sanction, pendant les quatre-vingt-dix jours suivant l’expiration. Cette fenêtre doit être coordonnée avec la date à laquelle les cinq ans sont réellement remplis. Si le client a beaucoup voyagé, le calendrier de dépôt doit aussi tenir compte de la continuité.

Le délai de décision est de trois mois. En l’absence de résolution expresse, le silence administratif peut être favorable. Mais ce silence ne produit pas automatiquement une carte physique. Il faut ensuite documenter la situation, obtenir la reconnaissance administrative nécessaire et gérer la prise d’empreintes et la cita TIE (https://legalfournier.com/fr/immigration-fr/citas-tie-2026-comment-obtenir-rendez-vous/). Cette étape est souvent sous-estimée, alors qu’elle conditionne l’exécution pratique de l’autorisation.

Le statut de longue durée est indéfini, mais la carte qui le matérialise se renouvelle. Confondre la durée du statut avec la validité physique de la TIE crée des erreurs de suivi, notamment chez les familles ou les clients qui voyagent beaucoup.

Pratique locale des Oficinas de Extranjería

Le cadre juridique est national, mais la pratique varie. Madrid, Barcelone, Valence, Alicante, Málaga et les provinces plus petites n’examinent pas toujours la continuité, les absences professionnelles ou les ressources économiques avec la même intensité. Les instructions ministérielles posent la base. La pratique de l’office compétent influence le niveau de preuve attendu.

Cette réalité est importante lorsque le client a changé de province. Le padrón, le domicile, la compétence administrative et les autorisations antérieures doivent former un ensemble cohérent. Un dossier préparé pour une province n’est pas toujours directement transférable à une autre.

Effets après obtention

L’autorisation permet de résider et travailler en Espagne de manière indéfinie. Elle donne une stabilité importante, mais elle ne met pas fin à toutes les obligations administratives. La carte physique doit être renouvelée, les absences longues doivent être surveillées et les changements significatifs de situation peuvent avoir des effets juridiques.

Pour les clients internationaux, la longue durée marque souvent un changement de perspective. L’Espagne n’est plus seulement un projet temporaire. Elle devient le centre de vie, de fiscalité, de patrimoine et parfois de structure familiale. Il est donc prudent d’aligner la stratégie migratoire avec la planification fiscale et patrimoniale.

Refus et recours

Un refus peut venir d’absences mal calculées, de documents étrangers défectueux, d’une voie UE choisie sans preuve suffisante, d’une assurance insuffisante ou d’une incohérence entre le passeport et la chronologie déclarée. Certains refus sont difficiles à éviter. D’autres auraient pu être anticipés avant le dépôt.

Après une décision négative, le client dispose généralement d’un mois pour un recours administratif de reposición et de deux mois pour la voie contentieuse administrative. Ces délais sont courts. Une fois dépassés, la résolution devient beaucoup plus difficile à contester et la stratégie doit souvent repartir du statut antérieur, si celui-ci reste viable.

Un recours solide n’est pas une lettre générale. Il doit répondre au motif précis du refus, reconstruire la chronologie, produire la preuve admissible et expliquer pourquoi l’interprétation de l’administration n’est pas correcte au regard du cadre légal.

Quand une analyse juridique est nécessaire

Nous recommandons une révision préalable lorsque le client a voyagé souvent, dispose de revenus variables, vise la modalité UE, possède des sociétés ou revenus dans plusieurs pays, a déjà reçu un refus, ou doit inclure des membres de famille dépendants. Dans ces situations, l’avocat ne prépare pas seulement un formulaire. Il choisit la voie, vérifie le calendrier, évalue le risque de refus et structure les preuves.

La prudence est également nécessaire lorsque le parcours comprend plusieurs régimes : étudiant, stage, travail à distance, non lucratif, compte propre, arraigo ou famille d’un citoyen de l’Union. Chaque transition doit être lue correctement pour éviter une erreur de calcul ou une rupture documentaire.

Questions fréquentes sur la résidence permanente Espagne

Qui peut demander la résidence de longue durée en Espagne ?

La règle générale vise les étrangers ayant résidé légalement et continûment pendant cinq ans. Des voies particulières existent pour certaines personnes nées en Espagne, anciens ressortissants espagnols et bénéficiaires de protection subsidiaire. La réponse pratique dépend toujours du dossier complet.

Les absences peuvent-elles bloquer la demande ?

Oui. Les absences doivent rester dans les limites admises. Si le total ou la durée d’une absence dépasse le seuil applicable, la continuité peut être remise en cause. Les voyages professionnels doivent être documentés avec soin.

Quelle est la différence entre la résidence nationale et la résidence longue durée UE ?

La voie nationale consolide la résidence en Espagne. La voie UE peut faciliter une mobilité ultérieure dans l’Union européenne, mais elle impose une preuve plus exigeante de ressources et d’assurance. Le bon choix dépend du profil documentaire.

Le statut expire-t-il ?

Le statut est indéfini, mais la carte physique doit être renouvelée. La perte ou le non-renouvellement matériel de la carte ne se traite pas comme une nouvelle demande de statut, mais il faut respecter les formalités et surveiller les absences longues.

L’administration peut-elle refuser après cinq ans de résidence ?

Oui. Cinq ans sont nécessaires, mais pas suffisants. L’administration vérifie la continuité, la légalité de la résidence, les antécédents, les documents étrangers et la cohérence de la voie choisie.

Conclusion : auditer avant de déposer

La résidence permanente Espagne donne une stabilité précieuse, mais elle ne doit pas être traitée comme une formalité automatique. Un dossier solide doit démontrer la durée, la continuité, la légalité de chaque période et l’adéquation entre la voie choisie et les preuves disponibles. Lorsque le client a un historique international, des voyages fréquents, des revenus variables ou une famille à inclure, l’audit préalable est souvent ce qui évite le refus.

Legal Fournier accompagne les clients internationaux dans l’analyse de leur dossier de longue durée : calcul des absences, choix national ou UE, documentation étrangère, preuve économique, assurance, recours et phase TIE.
