documents.title: Non-lucrative visa denied in Spain: appeal timing and evidence
documents.description: A denied non-lucrative visa in Spain is a deadline and evidence problem. Here is how to assess appeal timing, refusal reasons, and the appeal pack.
documents.text:
A non-lucrative visa refusal in Spain starts a deadline and exposes an evidence problem. The applicant must choose between reconsideration, judicial review and a better-prepared new filing. Read the refusal as a procedural document. Sending more documents without answering its legal reasoning is unlikely to resolve the problem.

This guide addresses a non lucrative visa Spain denied scenario: insufficient financial means, doubtful passive income, health insurance concerns, criminal-record or medical-certificate defects, unclear residence plans, missing apostilles or translations, or a consular conclusion that the file does not prove genuine non-working residence in Spain. Legal Fournier handles contested immigration files through our appeals service (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/appeals/), and can also review the evidence route through a focused consultation with a Spanish lawyer via our consultation route (https://legalfournier.com/en/start-consultation/?lf_cta_intent=booking).

A denial is a written administrative act. The appeal must answer the actual legal reason for refusal, preserve the deadline, and rebuild the evidence file around the current rules. Since May 2025, the core regulatory framework for this authorization is Royal Decree 1155/2024, so older online explanations based only on the previous regulation may miss the structure now being applied.

If the refusal concerns a non-lucrative route, compare the decision with the core Spain non-lucrative visa guide (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/spain-visa-non-lucrative/) before deciding whether an appeal or a corrected filing is stronger.

Published: 3 August 2026

The appeal clock normally starts from the day after notification of the refusal, not from the day the applicant first feels ready to respond.

Official Spanish consular pages commonly describe two routes: a reconsideration appeal within one month, and judicial review before the High Court of Justice of Madrid within two months.

Always read the denial notice first. The notice should identify the authority, the decision, the route of appeal, and the deadline applicable to that file.

An indexed legal and evidence pack usually works better than a long personal letter or the same documents uploaded again.

Under RD 1155/2024, non-lucrative residence turns on sufficient means, health insurance, no work or professional activity, and the general visa requirements.

In weak files, a new application may sometimes be more practical than an appeal, but only after checking deadline, jurisdiction, consular practice, and the risk of repeating the same defect.

Start with the refusal letter, not with the checklist

Most applicants first reopen the checklist and look for a document to replace. The instinct is understandable, but it starts in the wrong place. The appeal starts with the refusal letter: who issued it, when it was notified, whether it denies the visa, the residence authorization, or both, what legal basis it cites, and what factual conclusion it reaches.

For non-lucrative residence, the file has two connected layers. Article 39 of Royal Decree 1155/2024 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2024-24099) provides that the non-lucrative residence visa application carries with it the application for the corresponding temporary residence authorization. The consular office assesses the general visa requirements and, for this visa, the specific requirements in Article 61.2(a) and (b). The immigration office assesses certain other specific requirements. The final refusal may therefore reflect a consular concern, an immigration-office concern, or both.

An appeal that only says “I meet the requirements” is too vague. If the refusal says the financial means are not proven, the appeal must prove availability, ownership, regularity, amount, and credibility of those means. If the refusal says the health insurance is not adequate, the appeal must prove the insurer, the policy, territorial coverage, effective dates, payment, and any exclusions that matter. If the refusal cites missing legalization or translation, the answer is documentary, not rhetorical.

A denial is not a request to tell your life story again. It is a request to identify the legal defect found by the administration and answer it with admissible, organized evidence.

The current legal framework for non-lucrative residence

For applications in 2026, the current regulation is Real Decreto 1155/2024. Its transitional rules state that applications filed before the regulation entered into force are resolved under the rules in force when they were filed, unless the applicant requests application of the new regulation and meets the relevant requirements. The regulation also repealed the previous RD 557/2011 framework, so appeal work must check the filing date and the applicable legal regime before citing old article numbers.

Article 38 of RD 1155/2024 sets out general visa requirements. For example, the applicant must submit the visa form, not be irregularly in Spain, not be listed as rejectable in relevant territories, hold a passport or travel document valid for Spain with at least one year of validity, lack criminal records in countries of residence during the previous five years for conduct criminalized under Spanish law, pay the visa fee, and provide a medical certificate showing they do not suffer from diseases with serious public-health implications under the International Health Regulations.

Article 61 defines temporary non-lucrative residence as residence in Spain without carrying out work or professional activities. It also identifies specific requirements including sufficient economic means for maintenance and residence, health insurance, not being within an applicable commitment not to return, not representing a public order, public security or public-health threat, and payment of the procedure fee. The medical-certificate requirement sits in Article 38. Article 62 then explains the economic means test: 400% of IPREM for the applicant and an additional 100% of IPREM for each dependent family member, referred to the moment of the visa application or renewal. Because IPREM can change, appeals should calculate the threshold by reference to the amount in force on the relevant filing date.

Meeting the legal threshold is only the start. A consulate may examine whether funds are genuinely available, whether periodic income is reliable, whether the money belongs to the applicant, whether the evidence is recent, whether family members are correctly counted, and whether the applicant’s profile contradicts the promise not to work in Spain. A high bank balance can still fail if it is unexplained, temporary, borrowed, inaccessible, or inconsistent with the rest of the file.

Appeal timing: one month, two months, and the notice

Spanish consular pages for non-working residence visas usually state that, if a residence permit or visa is refused, the applicant may submit an appeal for reconsideration to the office that denied the request within one month from the day after notification. They also state that judicial review may be filed with the High Court of Justice of Madrid within two months from the day after notification of the refusal, or from dismissal of the reconsideration appeal.

Those consular statements sit against the general administrative and judicial rules. Law 39/2015 (https://boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2015-10565) regulates administrative appeals. Article 124 provides that a recurso potestativo de reposicion must be filed within one month when the act is express, and that the maximum period to decide and notify that appeal is one month. Article 30 explains how administrative time limits are counted: when a period is set in months, it is counted from the day after notification or publication, and if the final day is non-working, the deadline extends to the next working day.

Law 29/1998 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1998-16718), which governs contentious-administrative judicial review, sets the general two-month period for judicial review of an express administrative act. It also states that, where a reconsideration appeal has been filed first, the judicial-review period is counted from the day after express notification of that appeal’s resolution or from the day it should be deemed dismissed.

For the applicant, this produces three practical rules. First, keep proof of the notification date: email, electronic notice, consular letter, courier receipt, appointment record, or any other delivery evidence. Second, do not assume that “one month” means 30 calendar days. Month-based deadlines have their own counting rules. Third, do not file a superficial reconsideration appeal just to buy time if the case is really headed to court; a weak administrative appeal may damage the narrative and still leave the same evidence gaps.

Why non-lucrative visa applications are denied

Every file is individual, but most denials fall into a limited set of evidence categories. The legal requirements are not abstract. They have to be proven with documents that are current, properly legalized or apostilled where required, translated where required, and consistent with the applicant’s real life.

1. financial means are not credible enough

The non-lucrative visa is built for residence without work or professional activity in Spain. The appeal must therefore prove both amount and character of the funds. The applicant may need to show savings, pensions, dividends, rental income, investment income, company distributions, annuities, or other passive resources. If the file relies on employment income, remote work, active business services, or a promise to continue working while living in Spain, the evidence may contradict the nature of the authorization.

A strong appeal does more than attach a bank statement. It explains the source of the funds, the account holder, currency conversion, average balance, regularity of income, liquidity, restrictions on withdrawal, and whether family members are covered. For high-net-worth applicants, a wealth summary may help, but it should not replace transaction-specific proof. If money moved into the account shortly before filing, the appeal should explain where it came from and why it is genuinely available for residence in Spain.

2. health insurance does not match the requirement

Article 61 requires health insurance. Article 38 also includes the medical-certificate requirement. In practice, refusals can arise where the policy is not clearly valid in Spain, the insurer is not adequately identified, the coverage period does not match the intended residence period, proof of payment is missing, exclusions are unclear, or the policy document is not translated or formalized as requested by the consulate.

The appeal should include the policy certificate, general and special conditions where needed, insurer details, coverage dates, proof of payment, and a concise explanation of why the coverage satisfies the Spanish requirement. If the denial specifically refers to co-payments, waiting periods, territorial scope, repatriation language, or public/private coverage, the appeal must answer that exact point.

3. the criminal-record or medical evidence is defective

Article 38 requires lack of criminal records in the countries where the adult applicant has resided during the previous five years, for offences that exist under Spanish law. Official consular pages also regularly require legalization or apostille for foreign documents and official translation into Spanish where applicable. A denial may therefore come from the wrong country, wrong date range, missing apostille, non-accepted background-check format, uncertified translation, or mismatch between residence history and police certificates.

These defects are often fixable, but timing matters. If the appeal deadline is short and a new police certificate or apostille will take weeks, counsel may need to decide whether to file with evidence of the request, seek to supplement later where possible, or prepare a new application. The answer depends on the refusal wording and the consulate’s practice.

4. the residence plan looks inconsistent

A non-lucrative residence file should show a coherent plan to live in Spain without working. Problems arise when the applicant appears to be moving for remote work, continuing to manage a foreign company day to day, relying on active consultancy income, lacking a real Spanish address, applying with a family unit that is not well documented, or giving inconsistent answers at interview.

Drafting matters here. The appeal should not exaggerate or invent a lifestyle. It should describe the applicant’s real economic position in a way that fits the authorization: passive resources, retirement, investment income, family relocation, children’s schooling, private health coverage, Spanish housing plan, and any separation between ownership of assets and active work. For founders, executives, and investors, the file may need careful wording to distinguish shareholder income or governance from work or professional activity performed from Spain.

What counsel tests before recommending appeal or reapplication

The first question is whether the refusal rests on a correctable evidential gap, a legal disagreement, a credibility finding or facts that have changed since filing. That distinction affects both the available remedy and the evidence that can properly be used.

Counsel should compare the refusal notice with the original file, notification date and current circumstances. Financial means, insurance, foreign documents, residence plans and family calculations are reviewed for consistency. The resulting advice may favour an administrative appeal, judicial review or a new application, but the article cannot choose between them without the full record.

Appeal or reapply?

Not every denial deserves the same response. Reconsideration can work where the refusal is based on a misunderstanding, an overlooked document, a correctable formality, or a legal conclusion that can be challenged with a tighter explanation. A new application may be more efficient where the original file was incomplete, the applicant’s financial profile has materially changed, or the missing document could not realistically be obtained within the appeal window.

| Situation
| Appeal may fit when…
| New filing may fit when…

| Financial means
| The funds existed but were poorly explained or overlooked.
| The applicant did not meet the threshold or relied on active work income.

| Insurance
| The policy was valid but the document was incomplete or unclear.
| The policy genuinely did not cover the required Spanish residence period.

| Formal documents
| Apostille, translation, or certificate corrections can be produced quickly.
| Several core documents are missing and the file needs to be rebuilt.

| Work-activity concern
| The conclusion is wrong and passive-income evidence can prove it.
| The applicant’s real plan is remote work or active business from Spain.

Speed alone should not decide the route. An appeal creates a record. A poorly drafted appeal may confirm the administration’s concern. A new filing without understanding the denial may repeat the same defect and waste months. In complex family, wealth, or founder cases, the file may justify both: preserving the appeal deadline while preparing the next evidentiary route if the appeal is dismissed.

Special risk cases for wealthy families, founders, and cross-border applicants

A retiree with a pension and clean documents may have a mainly technical appeal. Founders, shareholders, wealthy families and internationally mobile applicants often present a different risk. The applicant may have enough money, but the file may not prove the right kind of money for a non-lucrative route.

Common examples include a founder who still owns and manages a company abroad, a family whose assets are held through trusts or holding companies, a spouse whose income supports the whole family but is not clearly available to the applicant, a recent property sale with funds moving through several jurisdictions, crypto-derived wealth converted into bank deposits, or a rental-income portfolio without clean tax and title evidence. These are not automatically fatal. They require a better evidence map.

The non-lucrative route also interacts with tax and residence planning. A successful visa is not the same as a complete tax strategy. Spending substantial time in Spain may trigger Spanish tax residence questions, foreign-asset reporting, wealth-tax exposure, inheritance planning, and banking evidence questions. The appeal should not casually describe facts that create unplanned tax consequences. For clients with property, family wealth, company ownership, or international income, immigration evidence and tax evidence should be aligned before the file is sent.

When the deadline makes review urgent

Urgency starts with the date and method of notification, not the date the applicant happens to read the decision. Preserve the refusal notice, notification record and complete application file, then obtain advice before a live appeal period is allowed to expire.

If there is no immediate deadline, review still matters where the refusal affects family travel, a property or relocation commitment, or a future residence application. See the underlying Non-Lucrative Visa requirements (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/spain-visa-non-lucrative/). Legal Fournier handles disputes through its appeals service (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/appeals/); a paid consultation (https://legalfournier.com/en/consultation-options/) is the starting point for a case-specific recommendation.

FAQ: non-lucrative visa denied in Spain

Can I appeal a denied non-lucrative visa in Spain?

Usually yes. Official Spanish consular pages commonly refer to a reconsideration appeal to the office that denied the request and a judicial-review route before the High Court of Justice of Madrid. The exact route and deadline should be confirmed from the denial notice and the facts of the file.

How long do I have to appeal?

Consular guidance commonly states one month for reconsideration and two months for judicial review, counted from the day after notification. Month-based Spanish deadlines must be calculated carefully under Law 39/2015 and the applicable judicial-review rules.

Can I add new evidence in the appeal?

Often the appeal includes corrected, clarified, or additional evidence, but it should be tied directly to the refusal reason. The safest approach is to explain whether the evidence proves a fact that already existed at filing, corrects a formal defect, or responds to a misunderstanding in the denial.

Is it better to appeal or apply again?

It depends on the defect. If the denial is based on a misread file or a fixable document issue, appeal may be appropriate. If the original application genuinely failed the economic, insurance, or non-work requirements, rebuilding and refiling may be more practical. The decision should be made before the appeal deadline expires.

Does a high bank balance guarantee approval?

No. The file must usually prove sufficient amount, availability, ownership, source, continuity, and compatibility with non-lucrative residence. A sudden or unexplained balance can create questions instead of solving them.

Legal Fournier support for visa appeals

Legal Fournier helps foreign applicants, families, investors, founders, and high-net-worth clients review refused Spanish immigration files and prepare appeal strategies. In a non-lucrative visa denial, our work usually starts with the refusal notice, the full original submission, the evidence trail, and a deadline calculation. From there, we assess whether the stronger route is reconsideration, judicial review, a new filing, or a combined preservation strategy.

If your non-lucrative visa has been denied in Spain, do not wait until the last week of the deadline to assemble documents from banks, insurers, foreign registries, translators, and apostille offices. Use our appeals service (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/appeals/) for contested immigration matters, or speak with a Spanish lawyer through our consultation route (https://legalfournier.com/en/start-consultation/?lf_cta_intent=booking) if you need a focused assessment before deciding whether to appeal or reapply.

Legal Fournier recommends seeking professional legal guidance before taking any action based on the information contained herein.

documents.title: Expulsion order in Spain: fines, appeals and proportionality defence
documents.description: A premium Legal Fournier guide to Spanish expulsion orders, when a fine may be proportionate, how appeals work and what evidence supports a proportionality defence.
documents.text:
A Spanish orden de expulsion is a removal decision, not another name for an immigration fine (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/multa-extranjeria-spain-fine-expulsion/). It can remove a person from Spain, create an entry ban affecting Schengen travel, extinguish an existing authorization and close pending residence or work files. Start with the procedure: identify what was notified, which deadline is running and whether the administration justified expulsion instead of a fine.

Advice on irregular stay often collapses into two claims: that it should only lead to a multa, or that expulsion is automatic. Neither is accurate. Spanish law allows expulsion for certain serious immigration infringements, including irregular stay under Article 53.1.a of Organic Law 4/2000, but the decision must be reasoned and proportionate. The Supreme Court’s current line treats a fine as the preferred response where no aggravating circumstances justify expulsion.

Legal Fournier reviews expulsion orders in the context of the whole file: entry history, notices, family ties, pending applications, employment, criminal or police records, previous immigration procedures and realistic regularisation routes. If you already have a resolution, the matter should be treated as an immigration appeal (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/appeals/), not as a general status question. If the issue started with a renewal or pending residence application, also review our residency renewal support in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/residency-renewal/).

Published: 21 July 2026 · Based on Organic Law 4/2000, Royal Decree 1155/2024, Law 39/2015, Law 29/1998, CJEU case C-409/20 and Supreme Court/CENDOJ summaries from 2023.

Before responding

Do not assume expulsion is automatic. For simple irregular stay, the current Supreme Court line treats the fine as preferred where no aggravating facts justify expulsion.

Fine and expulsion cannot be imposed together. Article 57.3 LOEX prohibits imposing both sanctions jointly for the same infringement.

The proportionality defence is evidence-led. Identity, entry route, family ties, pending applications, conduct and prior files matter more than generic hardship.

The procedure changes the clock. Ordinary expulsion procedures normally allow 15 days for allegations; preferential procedures can compress the first response to 48 hours.

Appeal deadlines run from notification. Reposicion and court routes have short periods. The exact resolution needs to be read before choosing payment, appeal or urgent suspension.

What an orden de expulsión does

An orden de expulsion is an administrative sanction that orders the foreign national to leave Spanish territory. In many cases it also carries a prohibition on entry. Under Organic Law 4/2000 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2000-544), expulsion can be used instead of a fine for certain very serious infringements and for specific serious infringements, including irregular stay, working without the required authorization in certain circumstances, concealment or serious falsehood, breach of security-related measures and participation in activities listed by the statute.

The order reaches beyond physical departure. Article 57 LOEX states that expulsion entails the extinction of any authorization to remain legally in Spain and the archive of any procedure intended to authorize residence or work for the expelled person. Article 58 adds that expulsion normally carries an entry ban, generally up to five years, with a possible longer period in exceptional public-order, public-security, national-security or public-health cases.

This is why a foreigner who receives an expulsion decision should not treat it as a standard administrative letter. A pending work authorization, family application, arraigo route, renewal, study modification or business plan can be affected by the order. The decision also matters for banks, employers, family logistics, travel and future Schengen entries.

Two questions matter: can the person avoid removal, and has the administration justified expulsion as the proportionate sanction for this file?

Fine or expulsion for irregular stay?

Irregular stay is a serious infringement under Article 53.1.a LOEX when a person is in Spain without having obtained an extension of stay, without residence authorization, or with an authorization expired for more than three months, provided they have not applied for renewal within the regulatory period. Article 55.1.b sets the ordinary fine range for serious infringements at 501 to 10,000 euros.

Article 57.1 then allows expulsion to be applied, in attention to the principle of proportionality, instead of the fine, after the relevant administrative file and through a reasoned resolution that assesses the facts configuring the infringement. Article 57.3 is equally important: fine and expulsion cannot be imposed jointly.

The controversy is whether a person in Spain irregularly should normally receive a fine or an expulsion order. After several CJEU and Spanish Supreme Court turns, the current working position is more balanced than the slogans suggest. The CJEU’s C-409/20 judgment (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX%3A62020CJ0409) accepted that, in the absence of aggravating circumstances, national law may initially impose a fine together with an obligation to leave, followed later by compulsory removal if the person neither regularises nor leaves within the prescribed period, provided the voluntary-departure framework respects the Return Directive.

The Spanish Supreme Court, as summarised in the official CENDOJ record for STS 4337/2023 (https://www.poderjudicial.es/search/sentencias/proceso%20para%20la%20proteccion%20de%20los%20derechos%20fundamentales/111/PUB), systematised the doctrine in 2023: irregular stay can lead to a fine or expulsion, with the fine preferred when no circumstances justify expulsion under proportionality. Where the administration chooses a fine, the resolution should also contain a voluntary departure order. Where it chooses expulsion, it needs an individualised assessment of aggravating circumstances that justify the more severe response.

The proportionality defence

A proportionality defence uses law and evidence to show that the file does not justify expulsion, or that the administration failed to explain why expulsion is proportionate instead of a fine. The defence should be built from the facts that existed and were documented in the administrative procedure, because a court may focus heavily on what the resolution itself used to justify the sanction.

Start with the aggravating circumstances relied on by the administration and test whether they are absent, weak or unsupported. A resolution that simply says “irregular stay” and then orders expulsion may be vulnerable if it does not identify facts that make expulsion proportionate. If the file alleges risk of absconding, lack of documentation, previous sanctions, a prior unexecuted expulsion, public-order concerns or obstruction of the procedure, those points must be tested one by one against the evidence.

Positive personal circumstances also matter, but they must be presented carefully. Family ties in Spain, minor children, school attendance, a Spanish or EU partner, a pending residence route, a clean criminal record, stable address, passport, medical or pregnancy circumstances, social roots, employment evidence and prior lawful entry can all be relevant. Their weight depends on the procedure and on whether they counter the specific reasons used by the administration.

For founders, professionals and internationally mobile families, the file may involve more than an overstay. A founder may have been waiting for corporate documentation, a spouse may have a pending EU family route, a family office may have submitted residence planning late, or a professional may have relied on a previous advisor’s renewal filing. These facts do not automatically defeat an expulsion order, but they can change the proportionality and remedy analysis.

Which procedure are you in?

The first document must be classified. An initiation agreement is different from a proposed resolution. A final expulsion resolution is different from a fine with an obligation to leave. A court judgment is different from an administrative act. Acting on the wrong assumption can waste the only useful deadline.

| Document or stage
| What it usually means
| Immediate legal task

| Acuerdo de iniciacion
| The sanction file has started.
| Identify whether ordinary or preferential procedure applies and calculate allegations.

| Tramite ordinario
| The ordinary sanction procedure is being used.
| Prepare allegations and evidence. Royal Decree 1155/2024 gives a 15-day period in the ordinary procedure.

| Procedimiento preferente
| Used for certain higher-risk situations, including specified public-order, absconding or obstruction scenarios.
| Act immediately. LOEX gives 48 hours for initial allegations and no voluntary departure period in those cases.

| Fine with obligation to leave
| A monetary sanction may be paired with a voluntary departure requirement.
| Review regularisation options and the exit deadline. A fine does not legalise the person.

| Final expulsion resolution
| The administration has ordered expulsion and usually an entry ban.
| Calculate administrative and court deadlines, assess suspension and build the appeal record.

Under Royal Decree 1155/2024 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2024-24099), sanction resolutions must be reasoned and, for sanction choice, the authority must value personal and family circumstances where Article 57 is engaged. The same regulation provides that ordinary expulsion resolutions include a voluntary compliance period, normally between seven and thirty days, while preferential expulsion resolutions are executed immediately according to their specific rules.

When a fine may be the correct outcome

A fine may be the correct or strategically preferable outcome where the file is essentially simple irregular stay and the administration has not proved aggravating circumstances of sufficient weight. This does not mean the person obtains a right to remain in Spain. It means the sanction is monetary, normally paired with an obligation to leave voluntarily unless the stay is regularised within the relevant period.

The fine route may be relevant where the person has a passport and stable address, entered lawfully, has no adverse record, did not obstruct the procedure, has Spanish family or social ties, has a pending or realistic regularisation route, and the administration has relied only on the fact of irregular stay. It may also be relevant where the alleged aggravating facts are not in the resolution, are unsupported by the file, or are too weak to justify expulsion.

However, the fine route is not a permanent shield. If the person does not regularise and does not leave, later proceedings may follow. A defence focused only on “give me a multa” can miss the rest of the file. Counsel must also assess any lawful route to status, the consequences of voluntary departure and whether an appeal provides useful protection or merely delays a weak case.

When expulsion risk is higher

Expulsion risk rises when the administration can point to facts beyond simple irregular stay. The law and case law do not reduce this to a closed checklist, but the risk analysis often focuses on identity, documentation, previous conduct, prior immigration files, public-order concerns, attempts to evade enforcement, employment infringements and whether the person can realistically be located during the procedure.

Article 63 LOEX allows preferential procedure for irregular stay where there is risk of non-appearance, where the foreigner avoids or hinders expulsion, or where the person represents a risk to public order, public security or national security. Article 62 also shows the kinds of factors a judge considers when authorising detention in an expulsion file, including risk of non-appearance due to lack of address or identity documentation, conduct aimed at hindering removal, prior convictions or sanctions and other pending criminal or sanction proceedings.

Those factors do not mean that every negative fact automatically validates expulsion. The administration must still motivate the decision and connect the facts to proportionality. A proportionality defence may accept that the stay was irregular while disputing that the additional facts are proven, serious, current or legally sufficient to justify expulsion.

Appeal routes and deadlines

A final expulsion resolution must state the available remedies, the competent body and the deadline. That text controls the immediate calendar. As a general framework, Law 39/2015 (https://boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2015-10565) provides a one-month period for an optional recurso de reposicion against express acts that put an end to the administrative route. Law 29/1998 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1998-16718) provides a general two-month period for contentious-administrative court appeals against express acts that put an end to the administrative route.

Those deadlines are short in practice. The lawyer needs the full notification, the administrative file if obtainable, the police report or initiation act, the proposed resolution, evidence submitted earlier, notification history, pending immigration files and proof of personal circumstances. If suspension is needed, it should be assessed immediately, especially where the procedure is preferential or the person is detained.

For a person outside Spain, the regulation provides that the relevant resources may be filed through diplomatic or consular representations, which will forward them to the competent body. That does not make the appeal simple; it makes documentation and timing even more important.

An expulsion appeal is usually won or lost on the administrative record: what the authority alleged, what evidence was before it, and whether the resolution explains why expulsion was proportionate.

Evidence to prepare before challenging the order

We normally start with a document map rather than a generic appeal template. The useful evidence depends on the ground for expulsion, but the core review often includes:

Identity and entry evidence. Passport, stamps, visa, tickets and documents showing lawful entry or explainable movement.

Status and filing history. Previous TIE, renewal receipts, pending Mercurio filings, family-card applications, arraigo files or rejection notices.

Notification record. How and when each act was notified, whether a representative was involved, and whether any deadline was missed.

Family and social ties. Marriage or partnership, children, school records, dependency, Spanish or EU relatives, registration and stable address.

Conduct evidence. Criminal-record certificates where appropriate, absence of prior sanctions, compliance with appointments and cooperation with the procedure.

Regularisation route. Whether a real legal path exists and whether it was already filed before the sanction file started.

The evidence should make the proportionality issue concrete: why the facts do not justify expulsion, why a fine or other handling would be legally more proportionate, or why execution should be suspended while a pending residence route is decided.

How Legal Fournier reviews the file

Classify the act. We identify whether the client has an initiation notice, proposal, fine, final expulsion resolution, court deadline or enforcement problem.

Calculate the live deadline. We work from the notification date and channel, not from when the client opened the email or understood the letter.

Read the stated reasons. We separate proven facts, legal classification, aggravating circumstances and generic wording.

Build the proportionality record. We gather evidence that weakens expulsion or supports suspension, regularisation or a fine outcome.

Choose the remedy. Depending on timing and risk, the next step may be allegations, reposicion, court appeal, urgent suspension, regularisation filing or a controlled voluntary-departure strategy.

This file leaves little room for trial and error: a missed 48-hour window, a weak appeal without suspension, or a document bundle that ignores the actual aggravating facts can turn a defensible case into an enforcement problem.

FAQ

Does an orden de expulsion mean I am banned from Spain?

Usually, yes, an expulsion resolution carries an entry ban. Under LOEX, the general maximum is five years, with an exceptional period of up to ten years for serious public-order, public-security, national-security or public-health threats. The exact period needs to be checked in the resolution.

Can I ask for a fine instead of expulsion?

In some irregular-stay cases, yes, the argument may be that the fine is the proportionate sanction because no aggravating circumstances justify expulsion. This is not automatic. The defence must address the facts used by the administration and the current Supreme Court line.

Can Spain impose both a fine and expulsion?

Article 57.3 LOEX states that fine and expulsion cannot be imposed jointly. A fine may still be paired with an obligation to leave, and later removal can follow if the person does not leave or regularise in the relevant period.

How long do I have to appeal an expulsion order?

The resolution must state the remedies and deadlines. Commonly, an express act ending the administrative route can be challenged by optional reposicion within one month or by contentious-administrative appeal within two months. Preferential and detention cases need urgent review because execution risk may be immediate.

Does a pending residence application stop expulsion?

It depends on the type of application, timing and procedure. LOEX contains specific rules for some exceptional-circumstances applications filed before the expulsion file. The CJEU also recognises that regularisation efforts can matter within the voluntary-departure framework. Do not assume every pending application suspends removal.

Can I appeal if I have already left Spain?

Yes, the current regulation contemplates filing administrative and judicial remedies from abroad through diplomatic or consular representations. In practice, evidence, powers of attorney, translations and timing must be organised carefully.

Legal Disclaimer. This article is provided for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Every case involves specific facts and circumstances that may affect the outcome. Legal Fournier recommends seeking professional legal guidance before taking any action based on the information contained herein.

documents.title: Immigration fine in Spain: when multa de extranjería replaces expulsion
documents.description: A practical guide to immigration fines in Spain, including how a fine differs from departure and expulsion, what evidence may matter, and why payment and appeal decisions depend on the exact notice.
documents.text:
A multa de extranjería is an administrative fine under Spain’s immigration rules. Paying it as though it were a routine bill can be a mistake. The notice may concern a proposed fine, a final fine, a requirement to leave Spain or an expulsion order (https://legalfournier.com/en/immigration/orden-de-expulsion-spain-fine-appeal-proportionality/). Each has different effects and may call for a different response.

Start by identifying exactly what was notified and when. A police report, initiation notice, proposed resolution, final resolution and proof of notification may each start a different procedural stage. The person’s immigration history, identity documents, ties to Spain and any pending residence application can also affect the analysis.

Position at 19 August 2026

Irregular stay is generally classified as a serious infringement under Article 53.1.a of Organic Law 4/2000.

Article 55 sets a fine of EUR 501 to EUR 10,000 for serious infringements. Article 57 permits expulsion instead of the fine in specified cases, subject to proportionality and a reasoned decision.

Supreme Court authority requires an individual assessment of aggravating circumstances before expulsion is chosen for irregular stay. Those circumstances must be identified and assessed in the administrative decision.

A fine is not a residence permit. The financial sanction must also be distinguished from any departure or return requirement in the operative part of the decision.

Payment consequences depend on the procedural stage and the wording of the notice. A pre-resolution reduction may require recognition of responsibility and withdrawal or waiver of an administrative challenge.

An appeal does not normally suspend execution automatically. The appropriate suspension or interim-measures request depends on the act and procedure.

Read the operative part before paying

Although a fine may be less severe than expulsion, it does not make an irregular stay lawful. It may sit alongside a requirement to leave voluntarily, and failure to comply may affect later enforcement. An expulsion order is different: it is imposed instead of the fine and may carry an entry ban.

Before paying or appealing, read the operative part of the decision. This is where you should find whether the document imposes money only, includes a departure requirement, orders expulsion, states an entry ban or records another consequence. It should also identify the available remedy, the authority or court before which it may be brought, and the time limit.

What Spanish law says about fines and expulsion

Article 53.1.a of Organic Law 4/2000 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2000-544#a53) classifies irregular stay as a serious infringement where the statutory conditions are met. For serious infringements, Article 55 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2000-544#a55) sets a fine of EUR 501 to EUR 10,000. It also requires proportionality in grading the sanction and makes the person’s financial capacity relevant to the amount.

Under Article 57.1 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2000-544#a57), expulsion may be imposed instead of a fine for specified serious or very serious conduct. The administration must use the appropriate procedure and issue a reasoned resolution that applies proportionality to the facts. Article 57.3 prevents a fine and expulsion from being imposed together as sanctions for the same infringement.

Not every case of irregular stay therefore ends in a fine. The administration must justify, in law and on the facts, why it has chosen expulsion. The person affected should check whether the alleged aggravating facts are established, relevant and assessed in the resolution, and should present any material favourable circumstances in time.

Fine, departure and expulsion are different

The three concepts are connected, but they are not interchangeable:

Fine: a financial sanction under Article 55. It does not grant or extend permission to stay.

Compulsory departure requirement: Article 28.3 of Organic Law 4/2000 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2000-544#a28) identifies situations in which departure is obligatory, including lack of authorisation to remain. A person may be given a period in which to comply voluntarily.

Expulsion: a separate sanction or return measure adopted through the relevant procedure. It may be executed voluntarily within a stated period in an ordinary procedure or enforced if the legal conditions are met. It can carry an entry ban under Articles 57 and 58.

The Supreme Court has explained that when irregular stay is sanctioned by a fine, the resolution should also include an order to leave that can be complied with voluntarily. This departure component is not the same as an expulsion sanction. The precise wording and procedural stage remain important because the Immigration Regulation approved by Royal Decree 1155/2024 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2024-24099) lays down distinct rules for compulsory departure, ordinary expulsion and immediately enforceable preferential expulsion.

Article 24 of the Regulation provides that a compulsory departure following certain refusal or lack-of-authorisation decisions must be completed within the period stated in the decision, or generally within a maximum of fifteen days from notification where that provision applies. For an ordinary expulsion resolution, Article 245 generally provides a voluntary-compliance period of seven to thirty days. A preferential expulsion procedure is different and may lead to immediate execution. A period that applies to one type of act should not be transferred to another.

Supreme Court authority on proportionality

The analysis should begin with the cited Supreme Court judgments, not a general case-law search. In Supreme Court judgment 1312/2023 of 24 October 2023, appeal 865/2022, ECLI:ES:TS:2023:4327 (https://www.poderjudicial.es/search/openDocument/261b2e4b0e775d3ba0a8778d75e36f0d), the Court applied the principle that a fine is preferred for irregular stay when no aggravating circumstances justify expulsion under proportionality. The judgment also addresses the need for relevant aggravating circumstances to appear in the administrative reasoning, instead of being added later as a new justification.

The Constitutional Court’s judgment 47/2023 of 10 May 2023, ECLI:ES:TC:2023:47 (https://www.boe.es/diario_boe/txt.php?id=BOE-A-2023-13958), explains how Spanish law relates to the EU Return Directive. It rejected the direct use of the directive against an individual to produce a harsher sanction not justified by Spanish law and the case file.

A fine is not guaranteed. Expulsion for irregular stay still requires an individual, reasoned proportionality assessment. A case without any properly established aggravating circumstance differs from one involving non-identification, evasion, non-compliance with a previous departure requirement or a properly evidenced risk to public order. Favourable circumstances also need to be considered in context; they should not be assumed to determine the outcome automatically.

Evidence that may be relevant

The notice and the proposed legal consequence determine which evidence is useful. No single checklist fits every case. The following categories are common.

1. Identity and travel history

A valid passport, previous NIE or TIE, consular records, entry stamps, visas and travel records may help establish identity, nationality and route of entry. The absence of one particular document is not automatically decisive. What matters is whether the administration can reliably identify the person and why any gap is relevant to proportionality or enforcement.

2. Address, family life and ties to Spain

Relevant evidence may include municipal registration, a tenancy, marriage or partnership documents, children’s records, dependent relatives, school enrolment, medical treatment and a documented history of residence. None of these facts automatically prevents expulsion. They may, however, be relevant to proportionality, family life and whether the person is likely to remain available to the authorities.

3. Pending residence applications

Document a pending application with its filing date, receipt, legal basis and current status. Article 240 of Royal Decree 1155/2024 contains specific coordination rules when an exceptional-circumstances residence application was filed before an expulsion procedure began. The effect is not automatic; it depends on the type, timing and merits of the application.

4. Work, study, health and vulnerability

Employment, self-employment, study, medical evidence, disability, pregnancy, care responsibilities and other documented vulnerabilities may all be relevant. Each document should be connected to a specific factual or legal point. Volume alone does not make an evidence pack persuasive.

Facts that may increase expulsion risk

The Regulation identifies circumstances relevant to using the preferential procedure for irregular stay. Article 233 refers to a risk of non-appearance, with factors including the absence of an address or identifying documents, lack of evidence of lawful Schengen entry or non-compliance with a compulsory departure requirement. It also covers conduct that avoids or obstructs expulsion, as well as risks to public order, public security or national security.

A decision cannot rely on labels alone. The administration must identify the supporting facts and explain their relevance. Police references likewise require care: a bare reference is not equivalent to a conviction or a reasoned assessment of specific conduct. The file should show what happened, the procedural status of any criminal matter and why the material is said to be relevant.

| Issue in the file
| Possible relevance
| Documents to consider

| Identity and entry
| Identification, travel history and availability to the authorities
| Passport, stamps, visas, tickets, consular records and previous files

| Address and family life
| Proportionality, family life and risk of non-appearance
| Municipal registration, tenancy, civil-status records, school and care evidence

| Pending application
| May affect procedure or a separate residence route, depending on timing and legal basis
| Filing receipt, case number, status and supporting documents

| Police or criminal material
| May be alleged as aggravating if specific, relevant and properly assessed
| Court status, dismissal or acquittal records, conviction and cancellation records, and context

Procedure affects timing and execution

Royal Decree 1155/2024 provides ordinary, preferential and simplified sanction procedures. The ordinary procedure generally moves through an initiation notice, a period for allegations and documents, evidence where appropriate, a proposed resolution, and a hearing before the final decision. The shorter preferential procedure may be used in certain expulsion cases, including irregular-stay cases involving circumstances listed in Article 233.

An expulsion file also carries rights to legal assistance and, where required, an interpreter. The final resolution must give reasons and state the available remedies, the competent body and the time limit. In a preferential procedure, Article 235 provides for the expulsion order to be executed immediately after notification, without removing the right to appeal. Prompt assessment of judicial interim measures is therefore particularly important.

Payment, reductions and waiver of an administrative challenge

The effect of payment depends on whether the document is an initiation notice, a proposed sanction or a final fine, and whether a statutory reduction is on offer.

Article 85 of Law 39/2015 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2015-10565#a85) states that once a sanction procedure has begun, recognition of responsibility may allow it to be resolved. If the sanction is only financial, or a non-financial sanction has been found inappropriate, voluntary payment before the final resolution may terminate the procedure. For an exclusively financial sanction, the initiation notice must specify the applicable reductions. These are at least 20 per cent for the statutory mechanisms and may be cumulative. Their effectiveness is conditional on withdrawal or waiver of an administrative action or appeal against the sanction.

Paying a final fine once it is final in the administrative route is a different matter. Article 252 of Royal Decree 1155/2024 states that immigration fines are enforceable once final in that route and generally must be paid within fifteen days of finality, unless suspended. Failure to pay may lead to enforcement proceedings.

Paying the financial amount neither grants residence nor, by itself, cancels a departure requirement. Before using a reduction or paying a final fine, check the exact act, the terms of the reduction, what must be recognised or waived, any remaining departure language and the person’s separate residence strategy.

Appeal periods depend on the act and notice

There is no single appeal period that can safely be applied to every immigration sanction. First establish whether the act is final or procedural, whether it ends the administrative route, whether it is express or presumed, which body issued it and when valid notification took place.

Under Articles 121 and 122 of Law 39/2015 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2015-10565#a122), an express act that does not end the administrative route may generally be challenged by an administrative appeal to the superior body within one month. Under Articles 123 and 124 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2015-10565#a124), an express act that does end the administrative route may generally be challenged by an optional reconsideration appeal within one month, or taken directly to court where permitted. Article 46 of Law 29/1998 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1998-16718#a46) generally provides two months for judicial review of an express act ending the administrative route.

These are general statutory periods, not a deadline calculation for a particular notice. Presumed acts, defective or unsuccessful notification, prior reconsideration, special procedures and non-final documents can change the route or calculation. Begin with the remedies section and notification record, then check them against the applicable law.

An appeal does not automatically suspend execution

Article 117 of Law 39/2015 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2015-10565#a117) sets the general rule that filing an administrative appeal does not suspend the challenged act unless another rule provides otherwise. Suspension can be requested when the statutory conditions are met, but it should not be assumed merely because an appeal has been filed.

In court, suspension or another interim measure also has to be requested and justified. Articles 129 and 130 of Law 29/1998 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1998-16718#a129) allow interim measures after the court weighs the interests involved and the risk that execution would defeat the legitimate purpose of the claim. Urgent measures are subject to their own procedural requirements.

Urgency depends on execution risk. A fine, an ordinary expulsion order with a voluntary-compliance period and an immediately enforceable preferential expulsion order do not carry the same urgency.

Submit evidence early, but assess later evidence carefully

Articles 227, 228 and 231 of Royal Decree 1155/2024 provide stages in the ordinary procedure for allegations, documents and evidence. Relevant material should be organised and submitted as early as reasonably possible, together with an explanation of what each item proves.

Do not assume that any document produced after the final decision will automatically be considered. Article 118.1 of Law 39/2015 (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2015-10565#a118) restricts reliance in an administrative appeal on facts, documents or arguments that could have been presented during the earlier allegations stage. In court, admissibility is governed by the rules and issues of the proceeding. A later document may still be relevant in some circumstances, but its admissibility and weight, as well as the explanation for producing it late, require a case-specific assessment.

File checklist before choosing a response

Before deciding whether to recognise responsibility, pay, appeal or seek suspension, collect:

the complete document received, including its remedies section;

proof of the date and method of notification;

the initiation notice, police report, proposed resolution and final resolution, if available;

passport, identity and travel records;

address, family, work, study, health and vulnerability evidence relevant to the alleged facts;

receipts and current status for any residence or protection application;

documents clarifying any police, criminal or previous immigration reference; and

a dated chronology of entry, expiry, applications, police contact, notifications and deadlines.

Record what is missing instead of filling the gaps with assumptions. A clear chronology and focused index are usually more useful than a large, unstructured bundle.

FAQ

Does an immigration fine legalise my stay in Spain?

No. A fine is a sanction, not a residence authorisation. Any residence route must be assessed separately. The decision may also contain a departure requirement.

Can Spain order expulsion for irregular stay?

Article 57 allows expulsion instead of a fine in specified cases, but requires proportionality and a reasoned, individual assessment. If no properly established aggravating circumstances appear, the Supreme Court’s case law supports the preference for a fine. The outcome depends on the actual decision and record.

Does paying the fine end the whole immigration issue?

Not necessarily. The effect depends on what is being paid, when, and whether a statutory reduction and waiver are involved. Payment does not grant residence and may not remove a separate departure requirement.

Does an appeal stop removal?

Not automatically. Administrative appeals generally do not suspend execution, and court proceedings also require an appropriate interim-measures request. The procedure and urgency must be checked immediately.

Can I submit new evidence after the decision?

Sometimes, but not always. Administrative and judicial rules can limit late evidence, especially when it could have been submitted earlier. Relevance, admissibility, timing and the reason for late production all need to be assessed.

Can I travel while an appeal is pending?

Do not assume that travel is safe. A departure requirement, expulsion order, entry ban, notification issue or residence status can affect re-entry and execution. Obtain advice on the exact file before leaving Spain.

Legal disclaimer. This article provides general information and is not legal advice. Immigration sanctions depend on the exact act, facts, procedure and notification record. Obtain advice on the relevant file before paying, waiving a remedy, travelling or allowing a deadline to pass.
