documents.title: Modelo 720 penalty notice: checks before paying or appealing
documents.description: A practical premium guide for foreign asset owners who receive a Modelo 720 penalty notice in Spain, including what to verify before paying, appealing or correcting the file.
documents.text:
A Modelo 720 penalty notice can expose more than the stated fine. For a person with foreign assets, the file may open the wider tax history: where the person was resident, how foreign accounts were funded, whether overseas securities were already taxed, and whether Spanish tax filings were coordinated with the information return.

Before paying or appealing a modelo 720 sancion, check whether the Spanish Tax Agency identified the correct obligation, asset category, data sets, penalty article and taxpayer. That review should happen before any payment decision, because prompt payment may resolve the immediate notice in one case but weaken the wider strategy in another.

Legal Fournier advises private clients, LATAM families and internationally structured entrepreneurs on Spanish tax exposure, foreign asset reporting and administrative defence. If the notice is connected to a wider move to Spain, inherited foreign wealth, company shares or real estate outside Spain, the matter should be reviewed with the broader family and tax position in mind. Our private client work for LATAM and Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/contact/) and our Talk to a Spanish lawyer (https://legalfournier.com/en/start-consultation/?lf_cta_intent=booking) are designed for exactly this type of international assessment.

If the filing obligation itself is in doubt, start with our Modelo 720 guide (https://legalfournier.com/en/tax-finance/modelo-tributario-720/), then move to the sanction notice and appeal grounds.

Published: 28 July 2026.

Current AEAT guidance states that Modelo 720 penalties are handled under the general penalty regime in articles 198 and 199 of the Spanish General Tax Law, not under the old specific fixed-penalty regime.

The old 150 percent penalty and uncapped fixed fines were condemned by the Court of Justice of the European Union in Case C-788/19 and Spain amended the regime afterwards.

A penalty notice should be checked against the three separate Modelo 720 information obligations: foreign accounts, foreign securities/rights/insurance/income, and foreign real estate.

Appealing a sanction in time usually suspends the sanction without a guarantee, but the treatment of a tax assessment or related debt can be different.

Payment can preserve certainty and sometimes reductions; appeal can protect against an incorrect or disproportionate penalty. The choice depends on the file, not on the headline amount alone.

Identify the document and legal basis

Modelo 720 is still associated with the former regime: extremely high fixed fines, a 150 percent sanction and the threat that an undeclared foreign asset could be treated as an unjustified capital gain without an effective limitation period. Those historic risks matter because they explain why many taxpayers are anxious when they receive a notice. They do not, however, tell you whether the notice in front of you has been correctly issued under the current law.

The Court of Justice of the European Union held in January 2022 that Spain’s earlier system went beyond what was necessary to protect tax control and prevent evasion. The official CJEU press release on Case C-788/19 (https://curia.europa.eu/jcms/upload/docs/application/pdf/2022-01/cp220018en.pdf) explains that the old limitation consequences, the 150 percent proportional fine and the high fixed fines created disproportionate restrictions on the free movement of capital. After that judgment, the current legal analysis is different.

The current AEAT FAQ on Modelo 720 sanctions and effects (https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/todas-gestiones/impuestos-tasas/declaraciones-informativas/modelo-720-decla_____sobre-bienes-derechos-extranjero_/preguntas-frecuentes/sanciones-efectos.html) states that the applicable sanctioning regime is now the general one in articles 198 and 199 of the Spanish General Tax Law. It also states that those penalties apply independently to each of the three information obligations contained in Modelo 720.

Start with the document received before choosing payment, appeal or a narrower position: a request for information, a proposed sanction, a final sanction, a tax assessment linked to undeclared income, a collection notice, or a combination of several acts. Each one opens a different response path.

What Modelo 720 actually covers

Modelo 720 is an informative return for certain assets and rights situated outside Spain. It is not itself an income tax return, wealth tax return or inheritance tax return. The problem is that an error in the information return can alert the Tax Agency to a larger tax issue if the asset values, income, funding history or ownership records do not match the taxpayer’s Spanish filings.

The official AEAT guidance on foreign income for Spanish residents summarises the three broad categories: accounts in foreign financial institutions; securities, rights, insurance and income deposited, managed or obtained abroad; and real estate or rights over real estate situated abroad. The same AEAT page states that the Modelo 720 obligation is generally fulfilled between 1 January and 31 March of the following year (https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/todas-gestiones/impuestos-tasas/declaraciones-informativas/modelo-720-decla_____sobre-bienes-derechos-extranjero_/plazos-presentacion.html), that each category has a EUR 50,000 threshold (https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/todas-gestiones/impuestos-tasas/declaraciones-informativas/modelo-720-decla_____sobre-bienes-derechos-extranjero_/preguntas-frecuentes/forma-calcular-limite-que-obliga-declarar.html), and that a later filing may be required when a previously reported category increases by more than EUR 20,000 (https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/todas-gestiones/impuestos-tasas/declaraciones-informativas/modelo-720-decla_____sobre-bienes-derechos-extranjero_/preguntas-frecuentes/frecuencia-presentacion-declaracion.html?faqId=8f40e5b0a9b8c310VgnVCM1000006986a8c0RCRD).

Those thresholds are often misunderstood. The EUR 50,000 test is not a single global test for all foreign wealth. It is reviewed by category. A person may have no filing obligation for foreign real estate but still have one for securities, or vice versa. After the first filing, the annual review asks whether there has been a reportable increase, a termination of ownership, or another reporting event under the applicable category rules.

For high-net-worth families, the difficult cases are often not obvious bank accounts. They are foreign brokerage portfolios with many lines, inherited interests, life insurance wrappers, usufruct rights, foreign companies, family trusts, nominee arrangements, or property owned through structures. A penalty notice based on one line of data may be pointing to a deeper classification problem.

Start with the obligation: a Modelo 720 defence starts with the precise reporting obligation, the asset holder, the valuation method and the evidence for the taxpayer’s position. The amount of the fine comes after that review.

The five checks before paying

When a client brings us a multa modelo 720, we usually separate the review into five questions. Factual and legal basics come before arguments about proportionality or EU law.

1. Was the taxpayer actually obliged to file?

The notice should be tested against tax residence, category thresholds, family status and the specific year. The AEAT FAQ confirms that persons who are Spanish IRPF taxpayers on their worldwide income can fall within the obligation. It also states that a person under the special inbound worker regime in article 93 of the IRPF Law is not obliged to file Modelo 720, although family members may be obliged if they are Spanish tax residents in their own right.

Executives, founders and internationally mobile families may have different tax profiles within the same household or structure. A spouse, adult child or family holding vehicle may have a different tax profile from the person who moved to Spain for work. A penalty addressed to the wrong person, or based on a year in which residence was not established, should not be paid without review.

2. Did AEAT use the correct asset category?

The current AEAT sanctions FAQ says each of the three information obligations is treated independently: accounts, securities/rights/insurance/income, and real estate. That independence can affect both whether there was an obligation and how a penalty is calculated. A portfolio of listed shares is not the same as a bank account. A foreign property is not the same as a right to receive income. A notice that mixes categories can inflate the calculation or obscure the real defect.

Virtual currencies require particular care. The consolidated text of the General Tax Law now refers to information obligations for certain virtual currencies abroad, but the AEAT procedure page for Modelo 720 warns that virtual currencies are not reported on Modelo 720 itself. If a notice or preparatory communication appears to mix crypto reporting with Modelo 720, the model and year should be checked carefully before any payment decision.

3. Is the value and exchange-rate position correct?

Valuation errors are common. The AEAT valuation FAQ explains that securities, accounts and real estate have specific valuation references, and that foreign currency balances normally need conversion into euros using the relevant exchange rate. For accounts, the balance at 31 December and average balance rules can matter. For foreign property, acquisition value and the effect of later exchange-rate movements may be treated differently from financial assets.

Broker statements and bank exports require careful reading. A platform may show market value, cash balance, cost basis and transaction value in different currencies. If the taxpayer or the Tax Agency selected the wrong figure, the penalty base may be wrong even if a filing obligation existed.

4. Is the sanction article correctly applied?

Under current AEAT guidance, a late or missing Modelo 720 is analysed through article 198 of the General Tax Law when there is no economic loss to the Treasury, while incorrect or incomplete data is analysed through article 199. The consolidated General Tax Law on BOE (https://boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2003-23186) states, in article 198, that failure to present information returns in time can be sanctioned by data or data set, with minimum and maximum limits, and that voluntary late filing without prior request can reduce the sanction and limits by half. Article 199 separately regulates incomplete, inaccurate or false declarations.

The notice should therefore show the legal basis, the number of data sets, the minimum or maximum applied, and whether the Tax Agency is treating the issue as late filing, non-filing, inaccurate data, wrong filing medium, or another form of non-compliance. If the notice jumps from an omitted value to a penalty amount without explaining the calculation, the calculation requires closer scrutiny.

5. Has culpability been justified?

Spanish tax penalties are not supposed to be automatic in the abstract. Article 179 of the General Tax Law recognises the principle of responsibility and excludes liability in certain cases, including where the taxpayer acted with necessary diligence, under a reasonable interpretation of the rule, or in line with published administrative criteria. Article 183 defines tax infringements as intentional or negligent acts or omissions that are classified and sanctioned by law.

A taxpayer cannot defeat every Modelo 720 penalty by claiming ignorance of the rule. The sanction file still needs reasoning rather than a bare conclusion. For a foreign client, relevant facts may include reliance on a Spanish tax adviser, ambiguity over residence, genuine classification doubt, conflicting platform data, prior voluntary correction, or evidence that the asset was fully disclosed elsewhere even if Modelo 720 was technically late or incomplete.

Pay, appeal or correct: the strategy matrix

There is no universal answer. A low, correctly calculated sanction with weak defence facts may be a payment case. A notice based on the wrong taxpayer, wrong category, incorrect calculation, poor motivation or an outdated legal theory may be an appeal case. A notice linked to undisclosed income or wealth tax exposure may need a broader regularisation strategy before the sanction question can be answered.

| Route
| When it can make sense
| Main risk

| Pay and close
| The obligation is clear, the amount is modest, the calculation is correct and wider tax risk is already controlled.
| Payment may accept a weak calculation or lose room to challenge if the file later expands.

| Appeal sanction only
| The penalty is poorly motivated, disproportionate in the specific facts, or culpability is weak.
| Appeal can affect reductions and requires a coherent evidence record.

| Appeal sanction and assessment
| AEAT links Modelo 720 to additional tax, alleged unjustified gains, wealth tax or another substantive tax issue.
| Debt suspension, guarantees and interest need separate analysis.

| Voluntary correction
| The taxpayer identifies an error before a formal requirement or before a wider inspection position crystallises.
| Late correction can still generate sanctions or invite questions if not documented properly.

Payment strategy should also include the reduction rules. Article 188 of the General Tax Law provides a 40 percent reduction for the amount of a sanction to be paid where the legal conditions are met, including payment within the applicable period and no appeal against the liquidation or sanction. The same provision states that the reduction can be demanded back if a timely appeal is filed against the liquidation or sanction. In plain English: a reduced payment is often a settlement choice, not a neutral procedural step.

Separate the commercial decision from the legal one. A family may choose to pay a defensible but small sanction to avoid distraction before a property purchase or relocation. Another client may need to appeal a larger notice because accepting the reasoning could damage a later year, a wealth tax position, or a future defence around asset origin.

Appeal timing and suspension

Tax notices are deadline-driven. The General Tax Law states that a recurso de reposicion is optional and, if used, must be filed before an economic-administrative claim on the same act. Article 223 gives a one-month period from the day after notification for the recurso de reposicion. Article 235 gives a one-month period for the reclamacion economico-administrativa in first or single instance. The exact deadline should always be calculated from the actual notification date and the specific act received.

The suspension point is especially important. Article 212 states that filing an administrative appeal or claim against a sanction in time and form suspends the execution of the sanction in the voluntary period without a guarantee until it is final in administrative proceedings. That is a major difference from many tax debts, where automatic suspension often requires guarantees or a separate suspension request. If the Modelo 720 file contains both a sanction and a tax assessment, they should not be treated as one single payment object.

For foreign clients, notification control is often the weak link. Electronic notifications, Spanish tax mailbox access, representative authority, travel and language barriers can compress the practical response time. Even a well-drafted appeal fails if the legal window has closed. The first operational step is therefore to preserve the file: download the notice, proof of notification, expediente, proposed calculations, prior communications and any previous filings.

Evidence that changes the outcome

The record determines the strength of a Modelo 720 penalty appeal. A strong file is organised, not emotional. It shows residence dates, the taxpayer’s status, the asset category, acquisition documents, account statements, the valuation method, exchange rates, prior tax returns, communications with advisers and any steps taken to correct the position.

For a foreign property, we would expect to review title, acquisition value, taxes and costs inherent to the purchase, ownership percentages and whether the property was held directly or through a company. For securities, we would review broker statements by year, ISIN-level data where relevant, market value, cash balances, account holder information and currency conversion. For life insurance or annuities, we would look at policy terms, surrender value and beneficiary rights.

Where the asset belongs to a foreign company, trust, foundation or estate, identify whether the Spanish taxpayer is holder, beneficial owner, authorised person, beneficiary, representative, person with power of disposal or another reporting subject under the relevant rule. These distinctions can decide whether the notice is correct, partially correct or addressed to the wrong person.

Clients who also own or manage Spanish companies should be particularly cautious. A Modelo 720 notice can connect with company formation, shareholder loans, director remuneration, dividends, foreign retained earnings or future investment into Spain. If your foreign asset issue is linked to a Spanish business plan, our guide to opening a company in Spain (https://legalfournier.com/en/business-in-spain/constitucion-de-la-sociedad-limitada/) may be a useful internal reference, but the penalty file should still be treated as a tax defence matter.

When to involve counsel

A simple late filing with a small sanction may be handled administratively. Specialist counsel is useful when the notice is substantial, when AEAT links the foreign asset to undeclared income, when the taxpayer’s residence is debatable, when family members or foreign entities are involved, or when the penalty reasoning is based on an old understanding of Modelo 720 law.

Counsel is also useful when payment looks commercially attractive but may damage the wider position. Paying a small sanction may look efficient, but if the underlying facts are wrong, the payment can leave a poor record for later years. Conversely, appealing every notice as a matter of principle can be expensive and unnecessary where the issue is clean, the amount is low and the client needs certainty.

Legal Fournier’s role in these cases is to map the exposure and choose a disciplined response: pay, appeal, correct, disclose, request the expediente, separate sanction from debt, or prepare a broader tax regularisation. The response should protect the client’s position without unnecessary litigation or friction.

Decision: do not decide from the payment letter alone. Decide from the full expediente, the calculation, the legal article, the proof of notification and the client’s wider Spanish tax position.

FAQ

Is the old 150 percent Modelo 720 penalty still the normal rule?

No. The old regime was condemned by the Court of Justice of the European Union in 2022, and the current AEAT FAQ refers to the general penalty regime in articles 198 and 199 of the General Tax Law. If a notice appears to rely on the old penalty logic, it should be reviewed carefully.

Can I appeal a Modelo 720 sanction without paying first?

Often, yes. Article 212 of the General Tax Law states that a timely administrative appeal or claim against a tax sanction suspends its execution in the voluntary period without a guarantee until it is final in administrative proceedings. This does not automatically solve the position for a related tax debt, so the documents need to be separated.

Will I lose reductions if I appeal?

It depends on the reduction and the act being appealed. Article 188 includes a 40 percent reduction linked to payment and not appealing. If preserving that reduction is important, the payment and appeal decision must be made before filing anything.

What if I was under the Beckham regime?

The AEAT FAQ states that a person under the special inbound worker regime in article 93 of the IRPF Law is not obliged to file Modelo 720. However, that answer does not automatically extend to all family members. Each person’s Spanish tax residence and filing status needs to be checked.

Is Modelo 720 the same as declaring foreign income?

No. Modelo 720 is an information return about certain foreign assets and rights. Foreign income, gains, wealth tax, inheritance issues or company distributions may require separate Spanish filings. A Modelo 720 notice can trigger those wider questions, but it is not the same filing.

Legal Disclaimer. This article is provided for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Every case involves specific facts and circumstances that may affect the outcome. Legal Fournier recommends seeking professional legal guidance before taking any action based on the information contained herein.

documents.title: Late Modelo 200 filing: corporate tax penalties for a Spanish SL
documents.description: A late Modelo 200 for a Spanish SL can trigger AEAT surcharges or penalties. The key is whether filing was voluntary, tax was due, and AEAT had already acted.
documents.text:
A late Modelo 200 can expose weak corporate governance, poor accounting control and wider Spanish tax risk. For a foreign-controlled company, the amount of the fine is only one part of the review. Check whether the company filed voluntarily, whether tax was due, whether AEAT had already contacted the company and whether the delay reveals another problem.

Founders, family groups and non-resident shareholders need to address the issue because Modelo 200 is the annual corporate tax self-assessment for the company. A dormant SL, a newly formed SL, a company with losses, and a profitable operating company can all be in very different economic positions, but the filing obligation still needs to be tested carefully. If the company was created as part of a relocation or commercial launch, the late return may also sit beside VAT, payroll, accounting, bank KYC or Spanish permanent establishment issues.

This is a corporate tax risk file, not a generic penalty calculation. If your SL is still being structured, start with our company formation in Spain service (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/company-formation/). If the company is already operating and needs ongoing tax control, our monthly accounting service (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/monthly-accounting/) is the more relevant starting point. This guide addresses the late filing of Modelo 200 by a Spanish limited company, often searched in Spanish as modelo 200 presentado tarde sanción sociedad limitada. It explains what may happen after a late filing and what to check before the company files or responds.

Published: 30 July 2026

Modelo 200 is the general annual Corporate Income Tax return for Spanish companies, and AEAT states that these returns must be filed electronically.

For calendar-year 2025 corporate tax returns, AEAT currently lists the filing period as July 1 to July 27, 2026, because the ordinary July 25 deadline falls on a Saturday.

If the company files late voluntarily and there is tax to pay, the usual issue is the Article 27 LGT surcharge, not an ordinary penalty: 1 percent plus 1 percent for each full month of delay before 12 months have elapsed; once 12 months have elapsed, 15 percent, with late-payment interest from the day after the 12-month period until filing.

If AEAT has already issued a prior requirement, the company is no longer in the same voluntary late-filing position; penalties can become materially more serious.

If there is no tax to pay or no economic damage to the Treasury, Article 198 LGT fixed penalties may be relevant, often lower where the filing is made late without prior requirement.

Corporate tax penalties, administrative fines and late-filing surcharges are not normally deductible expenses for Corporate Income Tax purposes.

What a late Modelo 200 means

Modelo 200 is not a simple annual information form. AEAT describes it as the self-assessment for Corporate Income Tax and, for certain cases, Non-Resident Income Tax involving permanent establishments and foreign pass-through entities with a presence in Spain. The AEAT Modelo 200 procedure page (https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/procedimientos/GE04.shtml) identifies it as the return and payment or refund document for these taxes. AEAT also explains in its Corporate Income Tax model guidance (https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/impuesto-sobre-sociedades/gestion-impuesto-sobre-sociedades/modelos-declaracion.html) that, as a general rule, Modelo 200 is the single model for Corporate Income Tax declarations and must be filed electronically.

For a Spanish SL, the return connects accounting, tax base, deductions, payments on account, withholding, refunds, balance sheet information and company status. A late filing raises three issues: whether the statutory deadline was missed, whether the return produced tax payable or another result, and whether the company filed before or after AEAT contacted it.

That chronology changes the legal treatment. A company that voluntarily files a positive return two months late is not in the same position as a company that ignores an AEAT requirement and only files after the administration has started a compliance action. A company with a zero result is not in the same position as a company that failed to pay EUR 80,000 of Corporate Income Tax. A dormant SL is not automatically exempt merely because it had no invoices.

Classify the file: before estimating the sanction, identify whether filing was voluntary or after a requirement, whether tax is payable, which tax period applies and whether this is an isolated mistake or a repeated pattern.

The deadline: why July 25 is not always the final day

The statutory rule is in Article 124 of the Corporate Income Tax Law. The consolidated BOE text of Law 27/2014 on Corporate Income Tax (https://boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2014-12328&p=20260321&tn=0) says the return must be filed within the 25 calendar days following the six months after the end of the tax period. Article 125 adds that taxpayers must determine the debt and pay it when presenting the declaration.

For most Spanish SLs whose accounting year matches the calendar year, this usually means the first 25 calendar days of July of the following year. But the actual calendar can move when the last day is a Saturday or holiday. AEAT’s 2026 Corporate Income Tax filing deadline guidance (https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/ayuda/manuales-videos-folletos/manuales-practicos/folleto-actividades-economicas/4-impuesto-sobre-sociedades/4_9-declaracion/4_9_1-plazo-presentacion.html) currently states that, for 2025 returns where the financial year coincides with the calendar year, the deadline runs until July 27, 2026. The same AEAT page states that direct debit for online filing is available from July 1 to July 22, 2026 for that 2025 return.

That distinction is important because a company may think July 25 is always the last day. In 2026, for a calendar-year 2025 return, AEAT’s own calendar points to July 27. In another year, or for a company with a different financial year, the answer may change. AEAT also explains that the tax period generally follows the company’s financial year, can be shorter in special cases such as extinction, change of residence or certain transformations, and can never exceed 12 months.

First fork: did AEAT contact the company first?

The most important factual question is whether there has been a requerimiento previo, a prior requirement or formal administrative action by AEAT. Article 27 of the General Tax Law, Law 58/2003 (https://boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2003-23186&p=20241221&tn=0), treats late self-assessments filed without prior requirement differently from cases where the administration has already acted. The law defines prior requirement broadly as an administrative action formally known to the taxpayer and aimed at recognition, regularisation, verification, inspection, securing or liquidation of the tax debt.

Filing before AEAT starts asking is usually more favourable. Once AEAT has issued a formal notice, the file can move into the sanction regime. This is why a late Modelo 200 should usually be filed proactively once the accounting and tax position are ready, instead of waiting to see whether AEAT notices.

For foreign directors, the risk is often practical: notifications may arrive through the electronic mailbox, at the tax address, or through an adviser who no longer manages the company. A director who says “we never received anything” may still face a valid notification problem if electronic notification access was not controlled. Before advising on the penalty exposure, someone must check the company’s notification history, certificate access, power of attorney status and AEAT mailbox.

Scenario 1: late voluntary filing with tax to pay

When a Spanish SL files Modelo 200 late, without prior AEAT requirement, and the return results in tax to pay, Article 27 LGT is usually the starting point. AEAT’s current guidance on late-filing surcharges (https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/ayuda/manuales-videos-folletos/manuales-practicos/irpf-2025/c18-cuota-liquida-resultante-autoliquidacion/regularizacion-situaciones-tributarias/recargos-aplicables.html) explains the modern rule: 1 percent plus another 1 percent for each full month of delay from the end of the filing and payment deadline, with no late-payment interest until the first 12 months have passed. After 12 months, the surcharge is 15 percent and late-payment interest accrues from the day after those 12 months until filing.

| Timing of voluntary late filing
| Typical Article 27 effect
| Practical note

| Within the first full month after the deadline
| 1 percent surcharge
| Do not delay while waiting for a notice if the return is ready.

| After 1 full month, but before 12 months have elapsed
| 2 percent to 12 percent surcharge
| The percentage rises with each complete month of delay.

| More than 12 months late
| 15 percent surcharge plus late-payment interest after month 12
| The time cost becomes materially worse after the first year.

The Article 27 surcharge regime matters because it excludes sanctions that could otherwise have been imposed for that voluntary late regularisation, and it excludes late-payment interest until filing within the first 12 months. AEAT also notes that the surcharge may be reduced by 25 percent if the Article 27.5 requirements are met. That reduction should not be treated as automatic without checking payment timing, notification, deferral or instalment conditions.

A company with a significant amount to pay must file correctly, choose between payment and deferral, and preserve the voluntary character of the correction. If the return is filed with wrong accounting, missing adjustments or an unsupported tax base, the company may solve the deadline problem while creating a later verification problem.

Scenario 2: late filing with no tax to pay

Many Spanish SLs miss Modelo 200 in years where there is no immediate tax to pay: early-stage losses, no activity, accumulated deductions, payments on account exceeding the final tax, or a refund position. That does not make the missed return harmless. The obligation to file is separate from the final amount due.

Where there is no economic damage to the Treasury, Article 198 LGT can become relevant. It covers failure to file self-assessments or declarations on time without economic damage. The general fixed fine is EUR 200. If the self-assessment or declaration is filed late without prior requirement, Article 198 says the sanction and limits are reduced by half. In many ordinary no-tax-due late Modelo 200 cases, that is why advisers often discuss a EUR 100 voluntary late-filing penalty, or EUR 200 if the filing occurs after AEAT has required it.

That said, the amount should not be quoted mechanically without reviewing the file. Was the return really zero, or did the company fail to include income? Was there a refund claim, a compensation of losses, an offset of payments, a special tax regime, or related-party information? Did the company file something incomplete before correcting it? Did AEAT issue a requirement? The fixed-penalty analysis assumes no economic damage and no more serious underlying non-compliance.

The dormant-company situation is especially common. A foreign shareholder forms a Spanish SL, does not trade immediately, and assumes no invoices means no corporate tax return. But an SL can still have accounting obligations, company status, shareholder transactions, bank movements, incorporation costs, deductible and non-deductible expenses, and a corporate tax filing position. Dormant should not mean unmanaged.

Scenario 3: AEAT requirement or tax not paid

If AEAT has already required the company to file, the Article 27 voluntary surcharge route may no longer be available for that obligation. The risk then shifts toward the ordinary sanction regime. The most serious common case is where tax should have been paid and was not paid on time.

Article 191 LGT regulates the tax infringement for failing to pay all or part of the tax debt that should result from a self-assessment. Depending on the facts, the infringement may be classified as minor, serious or very serious, and the proportional fine can range from 50 percent to 150 percent of the unpaid amount. The classification and graduation can depend on matters such as concealment, repeated infringements, fraudulent means, economic damage and other criteria in the General Tax Law.

A simple online answer is unsafe at this stage. If a company missed Modelo 200 but there is a large unpaid tax balance, possible hidden income, unsupported expenses, related-party transactions, missing withholding, cash movements, or a tax-address problem, the exposure is not just a fixed late-filing amount. The company may need a defence strategy, evidence pack and procedural review.

For directors abroad, the first task is to establish chronology. When did the tax period end? When did the filing period close? Was there any electronic notification? When was it opened or deemed notified? Was a draft or invalid return saved but not filed? Was payment attempted? Was a deferral requested? Was the company represented by a tax adviser with authority? The answer can change the entire penalty map.

What to check before filing late

A late filing still needs a complete accounting and tax review. AEAT’s Sociedades WEB guidance explains that the service allows electronic preparation and filing of Modelo 200, can import certain accounting data, validates the declaration, and may show errors, warnings and notices. Errors must be corrected before filing, while warnings and notices can often allow filing but should be reviewed because they may later lead to an AEAT requirement.

Before filing late, check the following:

Tax period: confirm whether the company uses the calendar year or another financial year, and whether there was extinction, residence change, transformation or another special event.

Accounting close: verify balance sheet, profit and loss account, shareholder accounts, director remuneration, bank balances and provisions.

Tax adjustments: review non-deductible expenses, limitation rules, prior losses, related-party pricing, withholding and payments on account.

Return result: determine whether the return is to pay, to refund, to compensate, or zero, because the late-filing consequence changes.

Notification history: check whether AEAT has already contacted the company before assuming voluntary filing treatment.

Payment route: decide whether to pay immediately, request deferral or instalment, or manage a payment issue before filing.

A late return is a tax position, not a single filing button. If the company sends a return with an incomplete accounting close because it wants to stop the clock, it may later need a rectification, complementary filing, or explanation. Article 122 LGT allows complementary self-assessments after the deadline where the legal conditions are met and the administration’s right has not prescribed, but this is not a substitute for preparing the original late return properly.

The connection with a Spanish permanent establishment

Modelo 200 can also apply beyond Spanish companies. Its Spanish permanent establishment implications explain why. AEAT’s Modelo 200 procedure also covers Non-Resident Income Tax for permanent establishments. AEAT’s help guidance for permanent-establishment taxpayers states that non-resident income taxpayers obtaining income in Spain through a permanent establishment may have to present the same model used by resident entities, Modelo 200, subject to the specific rules for those taxpayers.

For foreign founders, the Spanish SL and the permanent establishment question can overlap. A group may incorporate an SL after already selling, hiring, negotiating, storing goods, managing employees or signing contracts from Spain through a foreign company. If the SL then files Modelo 200 late, the delay may reveal only the newest problem. The older question may be whether there was an unreported Spanish permanent establishment or other Spanish tax exposure before the SL was ready.

This is why a late Modelo 200 for a foreign controlled SL should be reviewed with the operating timeline. Did revenue start before incorporation? Were contracts signed by the foreign parent while management was in Spain? Were local employees or dependent agents already active? Was the Spanish company invoicing correctly, or was the foreign company still collecting Spanish-source revenue? A penalty for late Modelo 200 may be manageable; an unresolved permanent establishment file can be much more sensitive.

Are the penalty and surcharge deductible?

For corporate tax purposes, the company should not assume that a late-filing surcharge or administrative penalty can simply reduce taxable profit. AEAT’s practical Corporate Income Tax manual section on fines, penalties and surcharges (https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/ayuda/manuales-videos-folletos/manuales-practicos/manual-sociedades-2025/capitulo-05-liquidacion-is-determinacion-imponible/bi-antes-reserva-capitalizac-compensac-00550/detalle-correcc-result-cuenta-perdidas-is/gastos-no-deducibles.html) refers to Article 15(c) of the Corporate Income Tax Law and states that criminal and administrative fines and penalties, enforcement-period surcharges, and late-filing surcharges without prior requirement are not tax deductible.

The accounting entry and the tax treatment are therefore not the same question. The company may record the cost in its accounts, but the corporate tax return may need a positive adjustment so the expense does not reduce the tax base. This is a common point missed by small SLs that handle the late penalty as just another supplier bill.

For foreign-owned companies, the non-deductibility point also matters commercially. A EUR 1,000 surcharge is not only EUR 1,000 of cash. It can create accounting clean-up work, board explanations, investor questions, bank KYC concerns and tax-adjustment tracking in a later Modelo 200.

How we review a late Modelo 200

We begin by reconstructing the file: company tax period, filing deadline, accounting close, return result, notification history, prior AEAT action, payment route, and whether any related obligations were also missed. For foreign controlled companies, we also review director residence, shareholder loans, group charges, bank KYC, payroll, VAT and any permanent establishment facts.

The record then determines the procedural route. If the company can still file voluntarily, the priority is to prepare a defensible late filing and control payment or deferral. If AEAT has already issued a requirement, the priority is different: respond within the procedural window, preserve evidence, assess penalties, and avoid admissions that create unnecessary exposure. If the return was filed but wrong, the question becomes whether a complementary or rectifying route is available and commercially sensible.

For ongoing control, Legal Fournier can coordinate the corporate tax calendar, accounting review and compliance pack through our monthly accounting service (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/monthly-accounting/). For founders still deciding whether an SL is the right structure, the better entry point is Spanish company formation (https://legalfournier.com/en/service/company-formation/). Where the issue is already live, a focused consultation with a Spanish lawyer can clarify the penalty exposure before filing, paying or responding.

FAQ

Is Modelo 200 late after July 25?

Not always. The legal rule is 25 calendar days after the six months following the end of the tax period. For many calendar-year SLs that usually points to July 1 to July 25. But if the last day is a Saturday or holiday, the deadline can move. For the 2025 Corporate Income Tax return, AEAT currently lists July 27, 2026 as the final day for calendar-year taxpayers.

What is the penalty if a Spanish SL files Modelo 200 late voluntarily?

If the late return is filed voluntarily, before AEAT requirement, and tax is payable, the Article 27 LGT late-filing surcharge is usually the starting point: 1 percent plus 1 percent for each complete month of delay before 12 months have elapsed; once 12 months have elapsed, 15 percent, with late-payment interest from the day after the 12-month period until filing. If there is no tax to pay and no economic damage, Article 198 fixed penalties may be relevant instead.

Does a dormant Spanish SL have to file Modelo 200?

Usually, yes. Lack of activity does not automatically eliminate the corporate tax filing obligation for an SL. The file still needs to be reviewed because there may be accounting entries, incorporation costs, bank movements, shareholder transactions or tax attributes that should be reflected correctly.

What happens if AEAT has already sent a requirement?

The company may lose the more favourable voluntary late-filing treatment for that obligation. Depending on whether tax was unpaid and on the facts, the case can move into the ordinary sanction regime, including Article 191 LGT penalties where tax that should have been paid was not paid on time.

Can the company deduct the surcharge or penalty?

Normally no. AEAT guidance on Corporate Income Tax states that administrative fines and penalties, enforcement-period surcharges and late-filing surcharges without prior requirement are not tax deductible under Article 15(c) of the Corporate Income Tax Law.

Why can a Spanish permanent establishment matter in a Modelo 200 article?

Modelo 200 can also be relevant for non-resident taxpayers with a Spanish permanent establishment. For foreign groups, a late SL return can sit beside a deeper question: whether the group was already operating from Spain before the SL was fully implemented. That should be reviewed separately from the fixed late-filing amount.

Legal Fournier recommends seeking professional legal guidance before taking any action based on the information contained herein.
